questions.stem: Before performing any ECG procedure, what should the technician verify first?
options: That a valid order from a licensed provider exists for that patient and procedure
That the patient has eaten in the last hour
That the patient has signed a HIPAA waiver
That the room temperature is above 75 °F
questions.explanation: Diagnostic procedures are performed only on a valid order from an authorized provider; the order tells you the procedure, protocol and any limitations. Eating, room temperature and HIPAA "waivers" are not prerequisites for an order.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: An order reads "ECG" but the patient tells you the cardiologist wanted a "stress test today." What is the best action?
options: Perform a stress test because the patient requested it
Cancel the ECG until the patient decides
Perform only what is ordered and contact the ordering provider to clarify
Perform both tests to save the patient a trip
questions.explanation: Technicians act within the written order. A discrepancy is clarified with the ordering provider before any additional procedure; performing an unordered test exceeds scope of practice.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: A treadmill order specifies "Modified Bruce protocol, hold beta blocker 24 h." The patient took metoprolol this morning. What should you do?
options: Proceed with a standard Bruce protocol instead
Give the patient caffeine to offset the beta blocker
Proceed without telling anyone because it is a minor issue
Notify the ordering provider or supervising physician before starting
questions.explanation: The order contained a patient preparation instruction that was not followed; the physician decides whether to proceed, reschedule or modify the test. Beta blockers blunt heart rate response and can reduce test sensitivity.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which item is NOT normally part of a complete ECG order?
options: Patient name and a second identifier
questions.explanation: An order identifies the patient, the test and who ordered it (and often the reason/diagnosis). Billing details such as copays are not part of a clinical order.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: An order for a pediatric patient requests "right-sided chest leads." Which lead set should you be prepared to add?
questions.explanation: Right-sided precordial leads (e.g., V3R, V4R) mirror the left-sided positions on the right chest and are commonly recorded in children and for suspected right ventricular infarction. V7–V9 are posterior leads.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The order says "STAT ECG." This means:
options: Perform it at the end of the shift
Perform it only if the patient has chest pain
Perform it immediately, ahead of routine work
questions.explanation: STAT (from Latin statim) means immediately. STAT ECGs, especially for chest pain, are prioritized; many protocols aim for an ECG within 10 minutes of arrival for chest pain.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A physician verbally orders a STAT ECG during an emergency. The best practice is to:
options: Refuse until a written order is entered
Perform the ECG but never document the order
Perform the ECG and ensure the verbal order is documented and authenticated per facility policy
Ask the patient to sign the order
questions.explanation: Verbal orders are accepted in urgent situations per facility policy, then documented and signed by the provider. Delaying an emergency ECG or failing to document are both inappropriate.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Patient limitations noted on an order (for example "non-weight-bearing left leg") are most important for:
options: Deciding which ECG paper to use
Choosing a safe procedure or protocol and transfer method
questions.explanation: Limitations affect how the test can be done safely (e.g., pharmacologic instead of treadmill stress, transfer technique). They do not change paper or filter choice.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for an exercise stress test cannot walk because of severe arthritis. The order should most likely be clarified to:
questions.explanation: Patients unable to exercise adequately are generally evaluated with pharmacologic stress (vasodilator or dobutamine). The physician must change the order; the technician should not substitute a test.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Which of these should you confirm on the order before a Holter hook-up?
options: Paper speed for the printout only
questions.explanation: Holter orders specify monitoring duration (commonly 24–48 hours) and sometimes indication. Treadmill speed and target heart rate apply to stress testing.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: If you find two orders for the same patient with conflicting protocols, you should:
options: Choose the newer protocol without asking
Ask the patient which they prefer
Hold and clarify with the ordering provider
questions.explanation: Conflicting orders are clarified with the provider; the technician does not choose between them.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: According to The Joint Commission, how many patient identifiers must be used before a procedure?
options: None if the patient is known to staff
questions.explanation: NPSG.01.01.01 requires at least two patient identifiers (e.g., name and date of birth) before procedures, medications or specimen collection.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: Which is NOT an acceptable patient identifier?
questions.explanation: Room and bed numbers are locations, not identifiers—patients move. Name, date of birth and medical record number are acceptable identifiers.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: The best way to verify identity with an alert patient is to:
options: Read the name on the door
Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth and compare to the wristband/order
Ask the visitor in the room
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions ("Please tell me your name and date of birth") avoid a confused patient simply agreeing. Compare the answers to the armband and the order.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: An unconscious ED patient has no armband. What should you do before recording the ECG?
options: Skip identification because it is an emergency
Label the ECG with the room number
Leave the ECG unlabeled and identify it later
Follow facility policy for temporary/unidentified patient identification (e.g., trauma alias and number) with the nurse
questions.explanation: Facilities use a temporary identification system for unknown patients so results stay linked to the right person. Room numbers or unlabeled tracings risk misidentification.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: HIPAA primarily protects:
options: The privacy and security of a patient's health information
questions.explanation: The HIPAA Privacy Rule sets national standards for protecting individually identifiable health information (PHI).
questions.source: U.S. HHS, Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule

questions.stem: A neighbor asks you in the cafeteria about your mutual friend's ECG result. You should:
options: Share it because the neighbor is a friend
Tell them to look in the chart
questions.explanation: Discussing PHI with people who are not involved in care violates HIPAA, even partial details. Only the patient or authorized persons may receive information, through proper channels.
questions.source: U.S. HHS, Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule

questions.stem: Which practice best protects PHI at an ECG cart?
options: Logging out of the device and not leaving printed tracings unattended
Posting tracings on the door for the physician
Leaving the screen showing the last patient
questions.explanation: Securing printouts and screens and using individual logins protect privacy and create an audit trail.
questions.source: U.S. HHS, Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule

questions.stem: Before printing or transmitting an ECG, the tracing must include at least:
options: The patient's name/identifier, date and time of recording
questions.explanation: Every tracing must be correctly labeled with identifiers and date/time so it can be compared with prior ECGs. Address and insurance are not needed on the tracing.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: You realize the ECG you just acquired was entered under the wrong patient. The best action is to:
options: Write the correct name over the printout
Notify your supervisor and follow the facility correction process so the record is fixed and the right patient is re-identified
Leave it; the physician will notice
questions.explanation: Misidentified records are a patient-safety risk. Report and correct them through the official process; never conceal or hand-alter records.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: A patient asks for a copy of their own ECG. Under HIPAA, the patient generally:
options: Has a right to access their records through the facility's release process
Can only get records with a court order
Must ask the technician to text a photo
questions.explanation: HIPAA gives individuals a right to access their health information. Requests go through the facility's release-of-information process rather than informal sharing.
questions.source: U.S. HHS, Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule

questions.stem: A patient rolls up their sleeve and lies down for an ECG after you explain the procedure. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Implied consent is shown by the patient's actions (cooperating after an explanation). Routine, low-risk procedures like a resting ECG usually rely on implied or verbal consent.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Which procedure most often requires signed informed consent?
questions.explanation: Stress testing carries a small risk of serious events, so written informed consent describing risks, benefits and alternatives is standard. Resting ECGs usually require only implied/verbal consent.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A competent adult patient refuses an ordered ECG after you explain it. You should:
options: Perform it anyway because it was ordered
Wait until the patient falls asleep
Respect the refusal, do not perform the ECG, and notify the nurse/ordering provider and document
Ask security to hold the patient
questions.explanation: Competent adults have the right to refuse care. Performing a procedure after refusal could be battery. Report and document the refusal.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A healthcare proxy (healthcare power of attorney) is used when:
options: The patient is too busy to sign
The patient lacks capacity to make their own healthcare decisions
questions.explanation: A healthcare proxy is a person legally designated to make healthcare decisions when the patient cannot. It is not a convenience for capable patients.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: In a life-threatening emergency when an unconscious patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available, care proceeds under:
questions.explanation: The law presumes a reasonable person would consent to emergency life-saving treatment (emergency exception/implied consent).
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Who is responsible for explaining the risks of a stress test and obtaining informed consent?
options: The physician/provider (or designee per facility policy), with the technician often witnessing
questions.explanation: Informed consent is the provider's responsibility; facility policy may allow a qualified designee. Technicians commonly witness signatures and answer procedural questions.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: For a minor (under 18, not emancipated), consent for a non-emergency stress test is usually given by:
questions.explanation: Minors generally cannot give legal consent for non-emergency procedures; a parent or legal guardian consents, although the child should still be given an age-appropriate explanation.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Which elements belong in informed consent for a stress test? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: Informed consent covers the purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives so the patient can make a voluntary decision. No outcome can be guaranteed.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Midway through a treadmill test, the patient says "I want to stop." The technician should:
options: Ignore it because consent was signed
Increase speed to reach target faster
Stop the exercise (begin recovery) and notify the physician—patient request is an indication to stop
Encourage them to finish the stage
questions.explanation: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, and the subject's desire to stop is an indication to terminate an exercise test.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Standard precautions are applied to:
questions.explanation: Standard precautions assume any patient may carry infectious agents and apply to all patient care.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: The single most effective way to prevent the spread of infection is:
options: Wearing a mask at all times
questions.explanation: Hand hygiene before and after patient contact is the most important infection-prevention measure.
questions.source: CDC Guideline for Hand Hygiene in Health-Care Settings (MMWR 2002)

questions.stem: A patient has Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) diarrhea. Which hand hygiene is preferred after care?
options: No hand hygiene needed if gloves were worn
questions.explanation: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. diff spores; washing with soap and water physically removes them. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
questions.source: CDC Guideline for Hand Hygiene in Health-Care Settings (MMWR 2002)

questions.stem: A patient with MRSA in a wound needs an ECG. Which isolation category applies?
options: Airborne precautions — N95 and negative pressure
questions.explanation: MRSA is spread by contact; contact precautions (gown and gloves, dedicated or disinfected equipment) apply in addition to standard precautions.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis needs a STAT ECG. You should wear:
options: Nothing—TB is not contagious by air
questions.explanation: TB, measles and varicella require airborne precautions: an N95 or higher respirator and an airborne infection isolation (negative-pressure) room.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: Influenza is transmitted mainly by large droplets. Which precaution applies?
options: Droplet precautions — surgical mask within close range
questions.explanation: Droplet precautions (a mask when close to the patient) are used for influenza, pertussis and similar organisms.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: Put the CDC sequence for DONNING (putting on) PPE in order.
questions.explanation: CDC sequence: gown first, then mask/respirator, then eye protection, then gloves (pulled over the gown cuffs).
questions.source: CDC, Sequence for Donning and Removing PPE

questions.stem: Put the CDC example sequence for REMOVING (doffing) PPE in order.
questions.explanation: CDC example: remove the most contaminated items first—gloves, then goggles/face shield, then gown, then mask/respirator—and perform hand hygiene immediately after removing all PPE.
questions.source: CDC, Sequence for Donning and Removing PPE

questions.stem: Lead wires and cables should be cleaned between patients with:
options: Bleach poured directly on the connectors
A facility-approved low-level disinfectant per manufacturer instructions
questions.explanation: Non-critical equipment that touches intact skin is cleaned with an approved disinfectant following the manufacturer's instructions. Soaking connectors or harsh chemicals can damage them.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: ECG equipment taken into a contact-isolation room should be:
options: Dedicated to that patient if possible, or thoroughly disinfected before leaving the room
Wiped only with a dry towel
Used on the next patient right away
questions.explanation: Contact precautions call for dedicated non-critical equipment or disinfection before use on another patient.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: Used disposable electrodes are discarded in:
options: Regular waste unless visibly contaminated with blood (then biohazard)
questions.explanation: Electrodes without blood go in regular trash per most facility policies; items soaked with blood or OPIM go in regulated (biohazard) waste. Sharps containers are for needles and sharp items.
questions.source: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030

questions.stem: If you are exposed to a patient's blood through a needlestick, your first action is to:
options: Ignore it if the patient looks healthy
Squeeze and apply bleach to the wound
Finish your shift and report the next day
Wash the area with soap and water, then report immediately per the exposure control plan
questions.explanation: Immediate washing and prompt reporting allow timely evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis if needed under the OSHA exposure control plan.
questions.source: OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030

questions.stem: When lifting, proper body mechanics include:
options: Hold the load at arm's length
Bend at the knees, keep the load close, and avoid twisting
Bend at the waist with straight legs
questions.explanation: Use leg muscles, a wide base of support, keep the load close to your center of gravity, and pivot with your feet instead of twisting the spine.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Before transferring a patient from a wheelchair to the exam table, you should first:
options: Raise the exam table to its highest position
Ask the patient to jump down
questions.explanation: Locking brakes prevents the chair from rolling away during the transfer. Lower the table and move footrests out of the way.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided weakness (hemiparesis) is moving from a wheelchair to a stretcher. Position the chair so the patient leads with:
questions.explanation: Patients transfer toward their stronger side so they can bear weight and control the move safely.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A patient feels dizzy when you sit them up after a stress test. The best action is to:
options: Return them to a supine or seated position, monitor, and notify the nurse/physician
Leave the room to get paperwork
Give them a cold drink and walk them out
Help them stand quickly so they can leave
questions.explanation: Dizziness may be orthostatic or a sign of a serious problem. Protect the patient from falling, keep monitoring, and get help.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A gait (transfer) belt is applied:
options: Around the patient's waist over clothing to help control a transfer
Around the patient's chest under the arms
Only after a patient has fallen
questions.explanation: Gait belts go snugly around the waist over clothing so the caregiver can steady the patient.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: When transporting a patient on a stretcher, the safest practice is:
options: Side rails down to allow comfort
Leaving the patient unattended in the hall
Side rails up and the patient's feet first in the direction of travel
questions.explanation: Rails up prevent falls; moving feet first lets the patient see where they are going and keeps the head protected.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A patient on a telemetry monitor must be transported for a test. Who should go with them?
options: Staff qualified per facility policy to monitor the rhythm and respond (often an RN or monitor-trained staff)
questions.explanation: Monitored patients may need personnel trained to recognize and respond to arrhythmias during transport, as defined by policy.
questions.source: Drew et al., AHA Practice Standards for Electrocardiographic Monitoring in Hospital Settings (Circulation 2004; update 2017)

questions.stem: Ergonomically, the ECG cart and bed height should be set so you can:
options: Lean over at the waist for long periods
Work without bending or reaching excessively
questions.explanation: Adjusting bed height and keeping equipment within reach reduces strain injuries. Kneeling, leaning at the waist for long periods, or reaching across the patient strain the back and increase injury risk.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: The angle of Louis (sternal angle) is used to locate the:
options: Second rib and second intercostal space
questions.explanation: The sternal angle is where the manubrium joins the sternal body; the 2nd rib attaches there. Count down from the 2nd intercostal space to find the 4th for V1/V2.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: V1 is placed in the:
options: 4th intercostal space at the left sternal border
4th intercostal space at the right sternal border
questions.explanation: V1: 4th ICS right sternal border. V2: 4th ICS left sternal border. A common error is placing V1/V2 too high (2nd–3rd ICS).
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: V4 is placed at the:
options: 5th intercostal space in the left midclavicular line
Anterior axillary line at the 4th ICS
questions.explanation: V4 is the anchor for the lateral leads: 5th ICS midclavicular line. V5 and V6 are placed level with V4.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: V3 is placed:
questions.explanation: V3 has no rib landmark of its own: place V4 first, then V3 halfway between V2 and V4. Midway between V1 and V2 or over the xiphoid are not standard sites; 5th ICS anterior axillary describes V5's line, not V3.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: V5 and V6 are placed on the same horizontal level as V4 at the:
options: Anterior axillary line (V5) and midaxillary line (V6)
questions.explanation: AHA recommendations place V5 at the anterior axillary line and V6 at the midaxillary line, level with V4 (not following the intercostal space upward).
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: For a female patient with large breasts, the AHA recommends placing V3–V6:
options: Under the breast on the chest wall, at the correct landmarks
On top of the breast tissue
One space higher to avoid the breast
questions.explanation: Electrodes should be placed on the chest wall beneath the breast rather than on breast tissue; lifting the breast gently (with explanation and permission) helps locate the landmarks.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to locate V1 correctly.
items: Palpate the sternal notch and slide down to the angle of Louis
Find the 2nd rib and the 2nd intercostal space beside it
Count down to the 4th intercostal space
Place V1 at the right sternal border in that space
questions.explanation: Locate the sternal angle → 2nd rib → 2nd ICS → count to 4th ICS → right sternal border for V1 (left sternal border for V2).
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Posterior lead V8 is placed:
options: At the left posterior axillary line
At the left paraspinal border, 2nd ICS
At the tip of the left scapula (mid-scapular line), level with V6
questions.explanation: Posterior leads are level with V4–V6: V7 posterior axillary line, V8 tip of the scapula (mid-scapular line), V9 left paraspinal area.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: V4R is placed at the:
options: Right midaxillary line at the 7th ICS
5th intercostal space in the right midclavicular line
questions.explanation: V4R mirrors V4 on the right chest. It is the most useful right-sided lead for right ventricular infarction.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Limb electrodes for a resting 12-lead are best placed:
options: On the chest near the clavicles for every resting ECG
On the limbs (arms and legs), on fleshy areas, symmetrically
questions.explanation: For the standard resting ECG, limb electrodes go on the arms and legs. Torso placement (Mason-Likar) is used for exercise testing and changes the tracing, so it must be noted if used.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Moving limb electrodes onto the torso (Mason-Likar placement) for a resting ECG may:
options: Make the ECG identical to a standard one
Alter QRS amplitudes and axis, so it should be noted on the tracing
Have no effect on the ECG
questions.explanation: Torso limb-electrode placement can shift axis rightward and change inferior-lead amplitudes; AHA recommends labeling such tracings as non-standard.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The standard patient position for a resting 12-lead ECG is:
options: Supine, relaxed, with arms at the sides
questions.explanation: Supine and relaxed minimizes muscle artifact and keeps the ECG comparable to prior tracings. If a patient cannot lie flat, use semi-Fowler's and note it.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A patient with severe shortness of breath cannot lie flat. You should:
options: Raise the head of the bed (semi-Fowler's) and note the position on the ECG
Force the patient to lie flat
questions.explanation: Patient safety and comfort come first; record the position since it can slightly change the tracing.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Put these skin-preparation steps in the best order.
items: Remove excess hair at the electrode site if needed
Clean the site to remove oils and lotion
Lightly abrade the skin if required
questions.explanation: Clip hair, clean with soap/water or alcohol, dry well, abrade lightly if needed (especially for stress/Holter), then apply the electrode with firm pressure.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Why is light skin abrasion recommended before stress testing and Holter monitoring?
options: It removes dead skin cells to lower skin impedance and reduce motion artifact
questions.explanation: The stratum corneum has high resistance. Light abrasion lowers impedance, improving signal quality during movement.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Body lotion on the chest should be:
options: Added to dry skin before electrodes
questions.explanation: Lotions and oils prevent electrode adhesion and cause artifact. Clean and dry the skin first.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Dry skin is a poor conductor of electrical current. This mainly causes:
options: Poor signal and artifact due to high impedance
questions.explanation: High skin impedance from dry skin weakens the signal and promotes artifact. CCI's sample questions highlight that dry skin is a poor conductor.
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: A cold, shivering patient will most likely produce which artifact?
questions.explanation: Shivering creates irregular, high-frequency muscle noise. Keep the room warm and cover the patient.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Before an ECG, the patient should be told to:
options: Hold their breath for one minute
Lie still, breathe normally and not talk during the recording
Tap their feet to stay alert
questions.explanation: Movement and talking cause artifact. Normal breathing avoids exaggerated respiratory baseline changes.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: For a patient with a below-the-knee amputation of the left leg, the left leg electrode should be:
options: Placed on the right leg with the RL electrode
Placed on the stump (or upper thigh) and the right leg electrode at the same level
questions.explanation: Place the electrode on the residual limb and keep the opposite limb electrode symmetrical. Note the modification on the tracing.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Electrodes should be checked before use for:
options: Moist gel and a valid expiration date
questions.explanation: Dried or expired electrode gel increases impedance and causes artifact. Store electrodes sealed and use them before expiration.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Mixing electrodes from different manufacturers on the same patient may cause:
options: Baseline offset and artifact because the electrodes have different electrical properties
questions.explanation: Different electrode chemistries can create half-cell potential differences that lead to unstable baselines; use matching electrodes.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Standard ECG calibration (standardization) is:
questions.explanation: The standard calibration pulse is 1 mV = 10 mm (two large boxes). Half-standard is 5 mm/mV; double is 20 mm/mV.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The standard ECG paper speed is:
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one small box (1 mm) = 0.04 s and one large box (5 mm) = 0.20 s. 50 mm/s is a special setting that doubles widths; 10 and 100 mm/s are not standard diagnostic speeds.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: If the calibration mark is 5 mm tall, the recorded QRS complexes will appear:
questions.explanation: At half standard (5 mm/mV), every deflection is half the height it would be at standard calibration; this must be noted when interpreting voltage.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The "sensitivity" (gain) control on an ECG machine controls:
questions.explanation: Sensitivity/gain sets how many millimetres per millivolt are recorded. (This is one of CCI's published sample questions.)
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: A recommended low-frequency (high-pass) filter for a diagnostic 12-lead ECG in adults is:
questions.explanation: AHA recommends a 0.05 Hz low-frequency cutoff (or equivalent linear-phase filter) to avoid distorting the ST segment, and a high-frequency cutoff of at least 150 Hz for adults.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Using a 40 Hz "monitor mode" high-frequency filter on a diagnostic 12-lead can:
options: Reduce QRS amplitude and smooth small notches, decreasing diagnostic accuracy
Have no effect on the waveform
questions.explanation: Lowering the high-frequency cutoff removes noise but also attenuates high-frequency QRS content; diagnostic ECGs need ≥150 Hz in adults.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Damaged or frayed lead wires should be:
options: Removed from service and reported for repair/replacement
Taped and used until they fail
questions.explanation: Damaged equipment causes artifact and electrical hazards. Tag it out of service per policy.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Routine electrical safety inspection of ECG machines is typically performed by:
options: Biomedical/clinical engineering per the facility schedule
questions.explanation: Biomedical engineering performs preventive maintenance and leakage current testing; technicians report problems and check for current inspection stickers.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: At a paper speed of 50 mm/s, one small box represents:
questions.explanation: Doubling paper speed halves the time per millimetre: 1 mm = 1/50 s = 0.02 s. Complexes look twice as wide.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Before a stress test, which equipment check is essential?
options: Confirm the treadmill is at maximum speed
Confirm the fax machine has paper
Confirm the room has a window
Confirm the defibrillator and emergency cart are present and functioning
questions.explanation: Exercise testing laboratories must have a defibrillator and emergency equipment/medications immediately available and checked.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which practice reduces the risk of electrical hazard to the patient?
options: Use properly grounded three-prong plugs and inspected equipment
Use extension cords and adapters freely
Place liquids on the ECG cart
Touch the patient and another device at the same time
questions.explanation: Grounded, inspected equipment and avoiding cheater adapters and spills prevent leakage current reaching the patient.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Patients with temporary epicardial pacing wires or central lines are at special risk from:
options: Microshock (small leakage currents reaching the heart directly)
questions.explanation: A direct conductive path to the heart means very small currents can cause ventricular fibrillation. Never touch exposed pacing wires and equipment at the same time.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A spilled cup of water near the ECG cart should be:
options: Ignored if the patient is stable
Cleaned up immediately to prevent slips and electrical hazards
questions.explanation: Wet floors are a fall risk and liquids near electrical equipment create shock hazards. Leaving it for later or covering it with paper still leaves a slip and shock hazard.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A confused patient keeps trying to get up during an ECG. The best way to keep them safe is to:
options: Keep side rails up as permitted, stay with the patient, and ask for help
Finish quickly and leave the bed in high position
Tell the patient to stay and walk away
questions.explanation: Fall prevention means staying with the patient, lowering the bed, using rails per policy and obtaining assistance; restraints require an order.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: During a routine ECG, your patient becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally. Your first action is to:
options: Call for help/activate the emergency response and begin CPR
questions.explanation: Recognize cardiac arrest, activate the emergency response system, start CPR and get an AED/defibrillator, per AHA BLS.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: For adult CPR, the AHA recommends a compression rate of:
questions.explanation: High-quality CPR: rate 100–120/min, depth at least 2 inches (5 cm) in adults, full recoil and minimal interruptions.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: A patient feels faint, becomes pale and sweaty after seeing the electrodes and slumps but is breathing with a pulse. This is most consistent with a vasovagal reaction. Best action?
options: Give them something to eat immediately
Lay the patient flat, elevate the legs if appropriate, monitor and notify the nurse
questions.explanation: Vasovagal syncope responds to lying flat with legs elevated to improve venous return. Keep monitoring and get help in case it is something more serious.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: The cord of the ECG machine runs across the walkway. This is a:
options: Trip hazard that should be rerouted
questions.explanation: Cords across walkways are trip hazards for staff and patients. It is never "good practice" or a grounding method—reroute the cord along the wall.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A latex-allergic patient needs a stress test. You should:
options: Use latex gloves but wash hands afterward
Use latex-free supplies (gloves, BP cuff, tubing) and alert the team
questions.explanation: Use latex-free products and communicate the allergy. Technicians do not administer medications without an order.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: When explaining a resting ECG, the most accurate statement is:
options: "The electrodes only record your heart's electrical activity; you will not feel any electricity."
"You will feel a small shock with each beat."
questions.explanation: A resting ECG is painless and quick. Reassuring patients that no current is delivered reduces anxiety and muscle artifact.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A patient asks you, "Is my ECG normal?" The best response is:
options: "Your physician will review the results and discuss them with you."
"I'm not allowed to talk to you."
"It looks like you had a heart attack."
questions.explanation: Interpreting results for the patient is outside the technician's scope; refer the patient to the provider courteously.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Typical pre-test instructions for an exercise stress test include:
options: Apply body lotion to the chest
Eat a large meal right before the test
Wear comfortable walking shoes and clothing and follow medication instructions from the physician
questions.explanation: Comfortable shoes and clothing, avoiding heavy meals and lotions, and following the physician's medication instructions prepare the patient for exercise testing.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Before a vasodilator (adenosine/regadenoson) stress test, patients are told to avoid:
options: Caffeine (coffee, tea, soda, chocolate, some medicines) for the specified period, usually 12–24 hours
questions.explanation: Caffeine and other methylxanthines block adenosine receptors and can make vasodilator stress ineffective.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Good patient education is best delivered:
options: In plain language, checking for understanding
questions.explanation: Plain language and teach-back (asking the patient to repeat key points) confirm understanding.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A patient who speaks limited English needs instructions for a Holter monitor. You should:
options: Use a qualified medical interpreter per facility policy
Ask the patient's 10-year-old child to interpret
questions.explanation: Qualified interpreters ensure accurate communication; using minors or untrained family members risks errors and privacy problems.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: During a stress test, the patient should be taught to report:
options: Chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness or other symptoms immediately
Only if they want a break
questions.explanation: Symptoms during exercise may indicate ischemia or arrhythmia and can be indications to stop the test.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which instructions are appropriate after a Holter monitor is applied? (Select two.)
options: Do not shower or get the recorder wet
Keep a diary of activities and symptoms with times
questions.explanation: Holter patients keep a time-stamped diary and keep the device dry; they should continue normal daily activities so symptoms can be correlated with rhythm.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Explaining the procedure before starting mainly helps to:
options: Reduce anxiety and improve cooperation, which reduces artifact
questions.explanation: An informed, relaxed patient moves less and produces a cleaner tracing. Explanation does not lengthen the test, change billing or raise the heart rate; it reduces anxiety-related artifact.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: How many electrodes are applied for a standard resting 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: Ten electrodes (4 limb + 6 chest) produce 12 leads: 3 bipolar limb leads, 3 augmented limb leads and 6 precordial leads.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: How many leads (views) does a standard 12-lead ECG record?
questions.explanation: Twelve leads are derived from ten electrodes. Lead = view; electrode = sensor.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Which item is NOT needed for a routine resting 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: A treadmill is stress-testing equipment. A resting ECG needs the machine, patient cable/lead wires, electrodes and skin-prep supplies.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The right leg (RL) electrode serves as the:
options: Ground/reference electrode used to reduce interference
questions.explanation: The RL electrode is a reference (driven-right-leg circuit) that reduces common-mode noise; it is not part of any lead's measurement.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Using AHA color coding, the right arm (RA) lead wire is:
questions.explanation: AHA (U.S.) colors: RA white, LA black, LL red, RL green. Memory aid: "white on right, smoke (black) over fire (red); snow over grass."
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using AHA color coding, the left leg (LL) lead wire is:
questions.explanation: AHA: LL red, RL green. "Smoke over fire" — black (LA) above red (LL) on the left side.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using IEC (international) color coding, the right arm electrode is:
questions.explanation: IEC colors: RA red, LA yellow, LL green, RL black. Know both systems because equipment varies.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using AHA color coding, V1 through V6 are colored:
options: Red, yellow, green, blue, orange, purple
Purple, orange, blue, green, yellow, red
White, black, red, green, brown, blue
questions.explanation: AHA precordial colors: V1 red, V2 yellow, V3 green, V4 blue, V5 orange, V6 purple (brown connector shell on many cables).
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A "three-channel" ECG machine:
options: Records only three leads in total
Records three leads simultaneously on the page
questions.explanation: Multi-channel machines record several leads at the same time (e.g., 3 channels × 4 columns + rhythm strip). A single-channel machine records one lead at a time.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: On a standard 12-lead printout in 3 × 4 format, each column of leads represents about:
questions.explanation: The page covers 10 seconds: four columns of 2.5 s each, often with a 10-second rhythm strip at the bottom.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Leads I, II and III are called:
questions.explanation: Each standard limb lead compares a positive and a negative electrode: I (LA+ vs RA−), II (LL+ vs RA−), III (LL+ vs LA−).
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Lead II measures between:
questions.explanation: Lead II: RA− to LL+. Its axis (+60°) roughly parallels normal atrial depolarization, which is why P waves are usually well seen and it is a common rhythm lead.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Lead III measures between:
questions.explanation: Lead III: LA− to LL+, oriented at +120°. RA→LL is lead II and RA→LA is lead I; LL is never the negative pole of a standard limb lead.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Einthoven's law states that:
options: Lead I + Lead III = Lead II
Lead I + Lead II = Lead III
questions.explanation: Because of the way the limb leads are connected, the voltage in lead II equals the sum of leads I and III at any instant. A tracing that violates this suggests a labeling or recording error.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Einthoven's triangle is formed by:
options: The SA node, AV node and bundle of His
Leads I, II and III around the heart
questions.explanation: The three bipolar limb leads form an equilateral triangle around the heart in the frontal plane.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: aVR, aVL and aVF are called augmented leads because:
options: They use extra electrodes on the chest
They are unipolar leads whose small voltages are electronically increased (augmented)
They are recorded at double paper speed
They measure only the P wave
questions.explanation: Augmented unipolar limb leads compare one limb electrode with the combined other two; the machine augments their amplitude by about 50%.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The precordial (chest) leads V1–V6 view the heart in the:
questions.explanation: Limb leads view the frontal plane; precordial leads view the horizontal plane, from right (V1) to left (V6).
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Normally, aVR shows:
options: Negative (inverted) P, QRS and T waves
questions.explanation: aVR looks at the heart from the right shoulder, so normal depolarization moves away from it; all waves are normally negative.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The frontal-plane angle of lead I is:
questions.explanation: Hexaxial reference: I = 0°, II = +60°, III = +120°, aVF = +90°, aVL = −30°, aVR = −150°. +60° is lead II, +90° is aVF and −30° is aVL.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The frontal-plane angle of aVF is:
questions.explanation: aVF points straight down (inferior), at +90°. 0° is lead I, +120° is lead III, and −90° is not the angle of any standard lead.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which leads are unipolar? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: Augmented limb leads and the precordial leads are unipolar; leads I, II and III are bipolar.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: On standard ECG paper, one small box horizontally equals:
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s each 1-mm small box = 0.04 s; each 5-mm large box = 0.20 s; 5 large boxes = 1 s.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: On standard ECG paper, one large box horizontally equals:
questions.explanation: A large box contains 5 small boxes: 5 × 0.04 = 0.20 s. 0.04 s is one small box; 0.40 s is two large boxes; 1.0 s is five large boxes.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Vertically, at standard calibration, one small box represents:
questions.explanation: 10 mm = 1 mV, so each 1-mm box = 0.1 mV. 1 mV is 10 small boxes (two large boxes); 0.5 mV is one large box.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: How many large boxes make up 6 seconds at standard paper speed?
questions.explanation: 1 s = 5 large boxes, so 6 s = 30 large boxes. Rhythm strips are often marked in 3-second intervals.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: QRS complexes in V2–V4 are so tall they overlap the leads above. The technician may:
options: Record at half standard (5 mm/mV) and clearly mark the change
questions.explanation: Half standard reduces amplitude to fit, but the calibration change must be shown on the tracing so voltages are interpreted correctly.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Low-voltage QRS complexes in an obese patient are hard to see. Which calibration makes them larger?
questions.explanation: Double standard (20 mm/mV) doubles deflection height; note the setting on the tracing. 5 and 2.5 mm/mV make waves smaller, and 10 mm/mV is the standard that is already too small here.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A rhythm strip was printed at 50 mm/s by mistake. Measured on the paper, the PR interval spans 8 small boxes. The actual PR interval is:
questions.explanation: At 50 mm/s each small box = 0.02 s, so 8 × 0.02 = 0.16 s. At 25 mm/s the same 8 boxes would be 0.32 s.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The calibration pulse appears rounded with "overshoot" at the corners. This usually indicates:
options: A stylus/damping problem with the recorder (on analog machines) needing service
questions.explanation: A square calibration pulse confirms proper frequency response; over- or under-damping distorts the corners and can distort waveforms.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The square pulse at the beginning of each row of a 12-lead ECG is the:
questions.explanation: The 1 mV standardization pulse shows the gain used for that recording. P waves, pacing spikes and artifacts are not square; the calibration pulse is a 1 mV reference.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A fine, regular, thick-looking baseline that makes waves look fuzzy is most typical of:
questions.explanation: 60-cycle interference is a uniform, regular high-frequency oscillation (60 per second in North America) from nearby electrical devices or poor grounding.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which action is most likely to reduce 60-cycle interference?
options: Ask the patient to breathe deeply
Unplug nonessential electrical devices nearby and check that the machine is grounded and cables are not crossing power cords
questions.explanation: AC interference comes from electrical fields: remove sources, keep cables away from power cords, check grounding and electrode contact.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: An irregular, jittery baseline appears when the patient is anxious and tense. This artifact is:
questions.explanation: Muscle activity produces irregular, random high-frequency deflections. Reassure the patient, keep them warm and supported, and have them relax their limbs.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: For a patient with a resting tremor (e.g., Parkinson disease), muscle artifact can be reduced by:
options: Placing electrodes on the hands and feet
Placing limb electrodes closer to the trunk (upper arms/thighs) and supporting the limbs
questions.explanation: Moving limb electrodes proximally (keeping symmetry) reduces tremor pickup. Some tremor can mimic arrhythmias such as atrial flutter.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A slowly drifting, up-and-down baseline that follows breathing is called:
questions.explanation: Wandering baseline is caused by respiration, movement, lotion or poor electrode contact. Check electrodes and skin prep; ask the patient to breathe normally.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: One lead suddenly shows a flat line while the others are normal. The most likely cause is:
options: A loose or disconnected electrode/lead wire
questions.explanation: If only one lead is flat or erratic, the problem is technical. Always check the patient first, then the electrode and wire.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The monitor shows what looks like ventricular fibrillation, but the patient is talking to you. What should you do first?
options: Check the patient and the electrodes/leads for artifact
questions.explanation: Treat the patient, not the monitor. A conscious, talking patient is not in VF—look for artifact (loose leads, movement, tremor).
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Put the troubleshooting steps for a poor-quality tracing in a logical order.
items: Check electrode contact and skin prep
Check lead wires and cable connections
Check the machine settings (filter, gain, speed)
Check the environment for electrical interference
questions.explanation: Start with the patient, then work outward: electrodes → wires/cable → machine → environment.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: On a 12-lead, lead I shows inverted P, QRS and T waves and aVR is upright. The most common cause is:
options: Reversal of the right and left arm electrodes
questions.explanation: LA/RA reversal inverts lead I, swaps II with III and aVR with aVL. Dextrocardia can look similar but also shows poor R-wave progression in V1–V6. Check electrode placement and repeat.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Which limb-electrode reversal produces an almost flat (very low amplitude) lead?
options: Swapping a leg electrode with an arm electrode involving the right leg (e.g., RA–RL)
questions.explanation: When RA (or LA) is swapped with the RL ground, one lead effectively measures between the two legs and becomes nearly flat. LA–RA inverts lead I; LA–LL is subtle.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Precordial electrodes placed one or two interspaces too high most commonly cause:
options: Poor R-wave progression or rSr' patterns that mimic infarction or RBBB
questions.explanation: High V1–V2 placement can produce rSr' and reduced R waves; correct landmarks avoid false findings.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A pacemaker patient's 12-lead shows no visible pacing spikes although the patient is paced. A likely reason is:
options: The ECG paper is upside down
Filters or a small bipolar pacing spike amplitude reducing visibility; many machines have a pace-detection setting
questions.explanation: Bipolar pacing spikes are small and may be filtered out; turn on pacemaker detection/enhancement if available and note pacing on the request.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Before blaming the machine for artifact, the technician should first:
questions.explanation: Patient movement, shivering, talking and poor contact are the most common causes of artifact.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Electrodes keep falling off a diaphoretic (sweaty) patient. The best fix is to:
options: Dry the skin thoroughly and use fresh electrodes, considering a skin-prep product
questions.explanation: Moisture prevents adhesion; dry the area, apply new electrodes and secure lead wires to reduce pull.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Hanging, heavy lead wires that pull on electrodes mainly cause:
questions.explanation: Tension on electrodes changes contact as the patient breathes or moves; support wires and use strain relief.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Put the steps for performing a resting 12-lead ECG in order.
items: Verify the order and identify the patient with two identifiers
Explain the procedure and obtain consent
Position the patient supine and prepare the skin
Apply limb and chest electrodes and connect lead wires
Enter patient data and record the ECG
Check the tracing for quality, then remove electrodes and clean equipment
questions.explanation: Order and ID → explanation/consent → position and skin prep → electrodes → enter data and record → check quality → remove and clean.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Why should the patient's age and sex be entered into the ECG machine?
options: Computer interpretation criteria (e.g., normal limits) depend on age and sex
questions.explanation: Automated algorithms use demographic data; incorrect entries can produce wrong interpretive statements.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A patient is having chest pain during the ECG. The technician should:
options: Complete the ECG promptly and immediately give it to the nurse/physician
Tell the patient to walk it off
Stop and wait until the pain goes away
Delay until the next routine run
questions.explanation: An ECG during symptoms is especially valuable. Finish quickly and alert the clinical team right away.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Why is V4 placed before V3 when applying chest electrodes?
options: The machine cannot record V3 until V4 is attached
V3 is defined as the midpoint between V2 and V4, so V4 must be located first
V3 must always be the last electrode applied
questions.explanation: Find V1/V2 (4th ICS), then V4 (5th ICS midclavicular line), then V3 halfway between V2 and V4, then V5 and V6 level with V4. Placement order is about landmarks, not about how the machine records or grounding.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: When comparing serial ECGs, consistent electrode placement is important because:
options: Changes in placement can create or hide differences that look like real changes
questions.explanation: Serial comparison relies on the same placement; marking electrode sites (per policy) can help.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The length of a standard 12-lead recording is:
questions.explanation: Standard 12-lead ECGs capture 10 seconds of data; longer rhythm strips are added for arrhythmias.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: An automated ECG statement reads "Acute MI—STAT" on a tracing with heavy artifact. The technician should:
options: Report the tracing immediately and, if appropriate, repeat a cleaner tracing—without telling the patient the interpretation
Tell the patient they are having a heart attack
questions.explanation: Computer statements must be confirmed by a physician; artifact can create false statements, but critical findings are reported promptly per policy.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The PR, QRS and QT values printed by the machine are:
options: Computer measurements that should be verified by the reader
questions.explanation: Machine measurements are generally accurate but can be wrong with noise or unusual morphology; physicians over-read them.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: For a patient with known dextrocardia, the modified ECG is recorded by:
options: Placing chest leads two spaces lower on the left
Reversing the arm electrodes and placing chest leads in mirror-image positions on the right chest
questions.explanation: Right-sided "mirror" placement (V1R–V6R) with arm-lead reversal shows the heart from its true position. Label the tracing clearly.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Right-sided chest leads are most useful to evaluate:
options: Right ventricular infarction in a patient with inferior MI
questions.explanation: ST elevation in V4R supports RV involvement, typically with proximal RCA occlusion during inferior STEMI.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Posterior leads V7–V9 are recorded to look for:
questions.explanation: ST depression in V1–V3 may reflect posterior injury; ST elevation in V7–V9 confirms it. Right atrial enlargement, pericarditis and pacemaker function are evaluated with the standard 12-lead or device checks, not posterior leads.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A 15-lead ECG commonly adds which leads to the standard 12?
questions.explanation: A common 15-lead configuration adds V4R (right ventricle) and V8–V9 (posterior wall). aVR, aVL and aVF and V1–V3 are already part of the standard 12-lead; no extra limb leads are used.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: When recording posterior leads with a 12-lead machine, you usually:
options: Move V4–V6 electrodes to V7–V9 positions and relabel the tracing
Turn the patient prone and leave labels as V4–V6
questions.explanation: Most machines have six chest channels, so V4–V6 are moved to V7–V9 and the tracing is relabeled manually or via a setting.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: For a pediatric ECG, which is true?
options: Adult filters must always be reduced to 40 Hz
Smaller electrodes may be needed and right-sided leads (V3R/V4R) are often included
questions.explanation: Pediatric ECGs often use smaller electrodes and right-sided leads; a parent's presence and a calm approach reduce movement artifact. Heart rates are normally faster than in adults.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A normal finding on a newborn's ECG that would be abnormal in an adult is:
options: Right axis deviation and right ventricular dominance
questions.explanation: Newborns have right ventricular dominance; axis normally shifts leftward over the first months to years.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: In a patient with a bandage over the V4 site, the electrode should be:
options: Placed as close as possible to the correct site, and the modification noted on the tracing
questions.explanation: Never place electrodes over dressings. Use the nearest possible site and document it so the reader knows the tracing is modified.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A Lewis lead (S5 lead) is a modified bipolar lead mainly used to:
options: Make atrial activity (P or flutter waves) more visible
questions.explanation: Placing the arm electrodes along the right sternal border (2nd and 4th ICS) enhances atrial activity to clarify wide-complex or atrial rhythms.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: MCL1 is a monitoring lead that approximates:
questions.explanation: Modified chest lead 1 places the positive electrode at the V1 position; useful for bundle branch block and P-wave morphology on monitors.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The positive electrode of lead aVL is on the:
questions.explanation: aVL: positive at the left arm (−30°); aVR at the right arm; aVF at the left leg. The right arm is aVR's positive pole and the left leg is aVF's; the right leg is the ground.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which lead is most perpendicular to lead I?
questions.explanation: Lead I is 0°, aVF is +90°. Perpendicular leads are used in the quadrant method of axis determination.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: On the hexaxial reference system, which lead is perpendicular to lead III (+120°)?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular leads differ by 90°: +120° and −150° (= +210°) are 90° apart. The pairs are I–aVF, II–aVL and III–aVR.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: If a wave of depolarization travels toward a positive electrode, that lead records:
questions.explanation: Current moving toward the positive pole is recorded upward; away from it, downward; perpendicular, biphasic or small.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A depolarization wave moving perpendicular to a lead produces:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular movement produces equal positive and negative parts—the basis for finding axis from the most equiphasic lead.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which setting combination is standard for a diagnostic 12-lead?
questions.explanation: Standard: 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, 0.05 Hz low cut and ≥150 Hz high cut for adults. The other combinations use non-standard speed, gain or monitoring-mode filters that distort the tracing.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A monitoring-quality filter (0.5–40 Hz) on a diagnostic 12-lead may artificially:
options: Distort the ST segment, causing false ST elevation or depression
questions.explanation: Raising the low-frequency cutoff above 0.05 Hz (without phase correction) can distort the ST segment, the most diagnostically sensitive part of the ECG.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Which type of electrode is standard for resting 12-lead ECGs today?
options: Copper wire wrapped on the wrist
questions.explanation: Disposable Ag/AgCl electrodes with conductive gel provide stable, low-noise contact. Needle, dry metal or wire electrodes are not used for routine 12-lead ECGs.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The patient cable "trunk" connects to:
options: The ECG machine, with lead wires branching to the electrodes
questions.explanation: Lead wires attach to electrodes and join at the patient cable connected to the acquisition unit.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: All 12 leads show heavy 60-cycle interference, even after unplugging nearby devices. The next most likely cause is:
options: A faulty or ungrounded machine, cable or outlet—report it to biomedical engineering
questions.explanation: Persistent, global AC interference points to grounding or equipment faults. Atrial flutter, tremor and heart block do not produce a uniform 60-cycle pattern in every lead.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A patient keeps talking during the recording. Which artifact is most likely?
questions.explanation: Talking and moving activate chest and arm muscles, adding noise. Ask the patient to stay quiet for the 10 seconds of recording.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which can cause a wandering baseline? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: Respiration, poor adhesion and lead tension shift electrode contact and baseline. A grounded machine and correct calibration do not cause baseline drift.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which actions reduce somatic (muscle) artifact? (Select two.)
options: Ask the patient to hold the bed rails tightly
Support the arms and legs so muscles relax
Turn on a nearby fan heater
Keep the patient warm and covered
questions.explanation: Warmth and relaxation reduce muscle activity; gripping rails and electrical heaters near the cables worsen artifact.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: How many chambers does the heart have?
questions.explanation: Two atria and two ventricles. (A CCI sample question.)
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and systemic arteries?
questions.explanation: The left ventricle ejects blood into the aorta for the systemic circulation. (A CCI sample question.)
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.explanation: The SA node in the right atrium fires fastest (60–100/min) and sets the rhythm. (A CCI sample question.)
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: Put the normal conduction pathway in order.
questions.explanation: Impulses start in the SA node, spread through the atria to the AV node (delay), then His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricular muscle.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Put the flow of blood through the right heart and lungs in order, starting from the body.
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood returns via the venae cavae to the RA, crosses the tricuspid valve to the RV and is pumped through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary arteries.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Put the flow of blood from the lungs through the left heart in order.
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the LA, crosses the mitral valve to the LV and leaves through the aortic valve.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?
questions.explanation: Right AV valve = tricuspid; left AV valve = mitral (bicuspid). Semilunar valves are aortic and pulmonic.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The innermost layer of the heart wall is the:
questions.explanation: From inside out: endocardium, myocardium (muscle), epicardium (visceral pericardium); the parietal pericardium surrounds the heart.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The P wave represents:
questions.explanation: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is usually hidden in the QRS.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The T wave represents:
questions.explanation: The T wave reflects recovery (repolarization) of the ventricles. Atrial depolarization is the P wave, ventricular depolarization is the QRS, and AV-node delay is part of the PR segment.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The PR interval mainly reflects:
options: Time from the start of atrial depolarization through the AV-node delay to the start of ventricular depolarization
Only the duration of the P wave
The time between two R waves
questions.explanation: The PR interval is measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS; most of it is the physiologic delay in the AV node.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Cardiac output equals:
questions.explanation: CO (L/min) = HR × SV. A typical resting adult CO is about 4–8 L/min.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: If stroke volume falls, the body maintains cardiac output initially by:
questions.explanation: Because CO = HR × SV, a compensatory tachycardia helps maintain output when stroke volume drops.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Stimulation of the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) generally:
options: Slows the heart rate and AV conduction
Has no effect on the heart
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic (vagal) tone slows SA-node firing and AV-node conduction; sympathetic stimulation speeds them.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The coronary arteries fill mainly during:
questions.explanation: The coronary ostia fill when the aortic valve is closed and the myocardium is relaxed—diastole. Fast heart rates shorten diastole and reduce coronary filling time.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Systole refers to:
questions.explanation: Systole = contraction/ejection; diastole = relaxation/filling. Relaxation and filling is diastole; "closure of the SA node" and repolarization alone are not systole.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The "atrial kick" contributes roughly what portion of ventricular filling at rest?
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction adds roughly 20–30% of ventricular filling; it is lost in atrial fibrillation, which can lower cardiac output.
