questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which coronary artery most commonly supplies the SA node and the inferior wall?
questions.explanation: In most people (right-dominant circulation) the RCA supplies the inferior wall, the SA node (~60%) and the AV node (~90%). This is why inferior MI is often associated with bradycardia and AV block.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The left anterior descending (LAD) artery supplies mainly the:
questions.explanation: The LAD supplies the anterior LV wall and anterior two-thirds of the septum (V1–V4). The inferior wall is usually RCA territory, and the right atrium is supplied by RCA branches.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The left circumflex artery mainly supplies the:
options: Lateral wall of the left ventricle
questions.explanation: The circumflex runs in the left AV groove and supplies the lateral wall (I, aVL, V5–V6) and sometimes the posterior/inferior wall.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Normal blood pressure in an adult, per the 2017 ACC/AHA categories, is:
questions.explanation: Normal is <120 systolic and <80 diastolic. Elevated: 120–129/<80. Stage 1 hypertension: 130–139 or 80–89.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Arteries carry blood ___ the heart; veins carry blood ___ the heart.
options: only to lungs; only from lungs
questions.explanation: Direction defines vessels. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart; pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood toward it.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Gas and nutrient exchange with tissues occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Capillaries are thin-walled vessels between arterioles and venules where exchange occurs. Arteries and veins have walls too thick for exchange; the venae cavae return blood to the heart.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which vessels regulate peripheral resistance most by constricting or dilating?
questions.explanation: Arterioles have smooth-muscle walls that control resistance and blood pressure. Capillaries and venules have little smooth muscle; the aorta is an elastic conducting artery.
questions.source: Shier, Butler & Lewis, Hole's Essentials of Human Anatomy & Physiology (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Inherent (intrinsic) rates: which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: SA node 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricles (Purkinje) 20–40 per minute. The fastest pacemaker controls the heart.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The interventricular septum normally depolarizes:
options: From left to right, producing a small septal q in I, aVL, V5–V6 and a small r in V1
questions.explanation: Initial septal activation from the left bundle moves left-to-right; LBBB reverses it and removes the septal q waves.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The normal QRS axis in adults is:
questions.explanation: Normal axis: −30° to +90° (some texts use 0° to +90°). Left axis deviation: −30° to −90°. Right axis deviation: +90° to +180°.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Using the quadrant method, QRS positive in lead I and negative in aVF suggests:
options: Left axis (check lead II: if II is negative, the axis is beyond −30°)
questions.explanation: Lead I + / aVF − places the axis between 0° and −90°. Lead II separates normal (−30° to 0°, II positive) from LAD (II negative).
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: QRS negative in lead I and positive in aVF indicates:
questions.explanation: Lead I − / aVF + puts the axis between +90° and +180°. Left axis needs lead I positive; normal axis needs both positive; extreme axis needs both negative.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: QRS negative in both lead I and aVF indicates:
questions.explanation: Negative in both places the axis between −90° and ±180°; consider ventricular rhythms, lead reversal or severe disease.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A common cause of left axis deviation is:
questions.explanation: LAFB is a classic cause of LAD (often −45° to −90°); inferior MI and LVH can also shift axis left.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A common cause of right axis deviation is:
questions.explanation: RVH, COPD/cor pulmonale, acute PE, left posterior fascicular block and normal infancy can produce RAD.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The most equiphasic (net zero) QRS is in lead aVL, and lead II is strongly positive. The axis is approximately:
questions.explanation: The axis is perpendicular to the equiphasic lead. aVL (−30°) is perpendicular to +60° (lead II), and II is positive, so the axis is about +60°.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The QRS is equiphasic in lead I and positive in aVF. The axis is about:
questions.explanation: Perpendicular to lead I (0°) is ±90°; aVF positive places it at +90°. 0° would make lead I most positive; −90° would make aVF negative; +180° would make lead I negative.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: An axis of −60° is classified as:
questions.explanation: −30° to −90° is left axis deviation. Normal ends at −30°; right axis is +90° to +180°; extreme is −90° to ±180°.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: An axis of +120° is classified as:
questions.explanation: +90° to +180° is right axis deviation. Normal ends at +90°; left axis is −30° to −90°; extreme is beyond ±180° to −90°.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Complete bundle branch block requires a QRS duration of at least:
questions.explanation: AHA/ACCF/HRS criteria: complete RBBB or LBBB requires QRS ≥120 ms in adults; 110–119 ms is "incomplete".
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: An rSR' ("rabbit ears") pattern in V1 with wide slurred S waves in I and V6 indicates:
questions.explanation: RBBB: late right ventricular activation gives a terminal R' in V1–V2 and broad terminal S in I, aVL, V5–V6.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A wide QRS with a deep QS or rS in V1 and broad, notched R waves without q waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6 indicates:
questions.explanation: LBBB: absent septal q waves and broad monophasic R waves laterally, deep S/QS in V1; ST-T changes are discordant (opposite the QRS).
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: In uncomplicated LBBB, the ST segments and T waves are typically:
options: Discordant—opposite in direction to the main QRS deflection
questions.explanation: Secondary repolarization changes oppose the QRS. Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm in LBBB is a Sgarbossa criterion suggesting acute MI.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: The "turn signal" memory aid for BBB uses V1: if the terminal QRS deflection points up, it suggests:
questions.explanation: Turn signal up (right turn) = terminal positive R' in V1 = RBBB; down (left turn) = negative = LBBB. Confirm with QRS ≥0.12 s.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: New LBBB in a patient with ongoing chest pain is significant because:
options: LBBB proves the patient is healthy
LBBB can mask or mimic ST changes of acute MI and the patient needs urgent physician evaluation
LBBB lowers heart rate to below 40
questions.explanation: LBBB alters repolarization, making ischemia hard to read. A new LBBB with symptoms is treated as a possible ACS and reported immediately.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Incomplete RBBB has an RBBB morphology with QRS duration of:
questions.explanation: AHA: incomplete RBBB has the RBBB pattern with QRS 110–119 ms in adults. ≥ 120 ms is complete RBBB; < 80 ms is normal; 200 ms is not a BBB criterion.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Bifascicular block most commonly refers to:
options: RBBB plus left anterior fascicular block
questions.explanation: RBBB + LAFB (or LPFB) involves two of the three fascicles; adding first-degree AV block is sometimes called "trifascicular".
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Sokolow-Lyon voltage criterion for LVH is:
options: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 ≥ 35 mm
R in V1 > S in V1
questions.explanation: Sokolow-Lyon: S V1 + R V5 or V6 ≥ 35 mm (at standard calibration). Cornell and other criteria also exist.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T-wave inversion in V5–V6 in a patient with tall voltages is called:
questions.explanation: The strain pattern reflects repolarization changes associated with LVH. Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, STEMI causes ST elevation, and pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A tall R wave in V1 (R > S) with right axis deviation suggests:
questions.explanation: RVH increases rightward/anterior forces: R ≥ S in V1, RAD and often right atrial enlargement. Posterior MI and RBBB are other causes of a tall R in V1.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Tall, peaked P waves (≥ 2.5 mm) in lead II suggest:
questions.explanation: Right atrial enlargement produces tall P waves in the inferior leads. Left atrial enlargement makes P waves wide and notched; AF has no P waves; hypokalemia causes U waves.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Broad, notched ("M-shaped") P waves ≥ 0.12 s in lead II suggest:
questions.explanation: Left atrial enlargement prolongs and notches the P wave; V1 often shows a deep terminal negative P component.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A common cause of left ventricular hypertrophy is:
questions.explanation: Pressure overload from hypertension or aortic stenosis thickens the LV wall. Asthma and low blood pressure do not create the pressure overload that thickens the LV.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Which factor can produce falsely high QRS voltage that mimics LVH?
options: Thin chest wall in a young athletic adult
questions.explanation: Young, thin patients often have high voltage without LVH. Obesity, effusion and COPD reduce voltage.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF indicates injury of the:
questions.explanation: II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall; inferior MI is usually caused by RCA occlusion.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Which leads view the lateral wall of the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: High lateral: I and aVL; low lateral: V5 and V6. Usually circumflex territory.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Leads V1 and V2 primarily view the:
questions.explanation: V1–V2 are septal; V3–V4 anterior; V5–V6 lateral. The inferior wall is II/III/aVF and the lateral wall I/aVL/V5–V6.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Leads V3 and V4 primarily view the:
questions.explanation: V3–V4 = anterior wall, LAD territory. Posterior changes appear as mirror images in V1–V3; high lateral is I and aVL.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: ST elevation in V1–V4 most likely indicates occlusion of the:
questions.explanation: Anteroseptal ST elevation points to the LAD. RCA occlusion causes inferior changes; circumflex causes lateral changes; the PDA supplies the inferior/posterior wall.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL with ST elevation in II, III and aVF supports:
questions.explanation: Reciprocal depression in leads opposite the injured wall supports a true STEMI rather than a benign pattern.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 should raise suspicion of:
questions.explanation: Posterior injury appears as a mirror image in V1–V3. ST elevation in V7–V9 confirms it.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Put the classic ECG evolution of an untreated STEMI in order.
items: ST returns to baseline; Q waves may persist
questions.explanation: Classic sequence: hyperacute T → ST elevation → Q waves → T inversion → ST normalizes with lasting Q waves. Reperfusion changes the timeline.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Ischemia (without infarction) classically causes:
questions.explanation: Ischemia affects repolarization (ST/T). Injury causes ST elevation; necrosis may leave Q waves.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A pathologic Q wave is generally one that is:
options: ≥ 0.04 s wide or ≥ 25% of the R-wave height (in leads where Q waves are not normal)
Any Q wave in lead aVR
questions.explanation: Wide (≥40 ms) or deep Q waves indicate prior infarction. Small septal q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6 and Q in aVR/III can be normal.
questions.source: Thygesen et al., Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

questions.stem: Per the Universal Definition of MI, new ST elevation at the J point in V2–V3 in a man 40 years or older meets STEMI criteria at:
questions.explanation: In V2–V3: ≥2 mm in men ≥40, ≥2.5 mm in men <40, ≥1.5 mm in women. Other leads: ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads.
questions.source: Thygesen et al., Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

questions.stem: ST elevation is measured at the:
options: J point (end of the QRS), compared with the baseline (PR/TP segment)
questions.explanation: The J point is the junction between the QRS and ST segment; elevation is referenced to the isoelectric baseline.
questions.source: Thygesen et al., Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

questions.stem: Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R suggests:
questions.explanation: V4R ST elevation ≥1 mm indicates RV involvement, which matters because these patients are preload dependent (nitrates can drop BP).
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Diffuse concave ST elevation in most leads with PR depression and no reciprocal changes (except aVR) suggests:
questions.explanation: Pericarditis causes widespread ST elevation and PR depression; aVR often shows PR elevation and ST depression.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which lead group would show ST elevation in a "high lateral" MI?
questions.explanation: High lateral wall is seen by I and aVL, often first diagonal or circumflex branch. II/III/aVF are inferior, V1–V2 are septal and V3R–V4R are right-sided.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: A patient with an acute inferior MI develops a heart rate of 40 with second-degree AV block. This is most likely because:
options: The RCA supplies the AV node in most people
The LAD supplies the SA node
The patient is on a treadmill
questions.explanation: Inferior MI (RCA) commonly causes sinus bradycardia and AV-nodal block (e.g., Mobitz I), often transient.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which leads are "contiguous" with lead III? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: Contiguous leads view the same region: II, III and aVF are the inferior group. aVL faces the high lateral wall and V1/V6 are precordial leads in other regions.
questions.source: Thygesen et al., Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

questions.stem: Which leads make up the anterior/septal (LAD) territory? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: V1–V4 reflect septal and anterior regions supplied by the LAD. II and aVF are inferior; aVL is high lateral.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality produces tall, narrow, peaked T waves?
questions.explanation: Early hyperkalemia peaks the T waves; worsening levels widen the QRS, flatten P waves and can cause a sine-wave pattern and arrest.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Prominent U waves with flattened T waves suggest:
questions.explanation: Low potassium flattens T waves, produces U waves and can lengthen the QU interval. Hyperkalemia peaks the T waves, hypercalcemia shortens QT, and pericarditis elevates ST segments.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Hypercalcemia typically causes a:
questions.explanation: High calcium shortens the ST segment and QT; low calcium lengthens it. A long QT suggests hypocalcemia; peaked P waves suggest right atrial enlargement; delta waves suggest WPW.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A short PR interval (< 0.12 s), a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke) and a widened QRS suggest:
questions.explanation: An accessory pathway bypasses the AV node, pre-exciting the ventricles. WPW predisposes to reentrant tachycardias.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Poor R-wave progression across V1–V4 can be caused by:
options: Prior anterior MI or incorrect (high) chest-lead placement
questions.explanation: R waves normally grow from V1 to V4–V5. Absent progression may be from old anterior infarction, LVH, LBBB, COPD or electrode misplacement.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: R-wave progression: the "transition zone," where R and S waves are about equal, is normally in:
questions.explanation: R waves grow and S waves shrink across the precordium, with transition usually at V3–V4. V1 normally shows a small r with a deep S, and V6 a dominant R; aVR is a limb lead.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which wall is NOT directly viewed by any standard 12-lead lead?
questions.explanation: No standard lead faces the posterior wall; it is inferred from reciprocal changes in V1–V3 or recorded with V7–V9.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Wellens' syndrome (deep symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 in a pain-free patient) is important because it suggests:
options: Critical proximal LAD stenosis at high risk of anterior MI
questions.explanation: Wellens' T waves indicate a critical LAD lesion; stress testing is generally avoided and the finding is reported urgently.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Normal QTc for adults is generally considered less than about:
questions.explanation: Thresholds vary by source; AHA uses ≥450 ms (men) and ≥460 ms (women) as prolonged. QTc >500 ms is high risk for torsades.
questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Bazett's formula corrects the QT interval using:
questions.explanation: Bazett: QTc = QT/√RR. At 60 bpm (RR = 1 s), QTc = QT.
questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Digoxin at therapeutic levels commonly causes:
options: Scooped ("sagging") ST depression and a shortened QT
questions.explanation: The "digoxin effect" (Salvador Dalí mustache ST) is expected and not toxicity by itself. Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia, delta waves WPW, and ST elevation V1–V4 anterior injury.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which item must be immediately available in every exercise testing laboratory?
options: A defibrillator and emergency (crash) cart with medications
questions.explanation: Serious events are rare but possible; a defibrillator, airway equipment and emergency drugs must be present and checked, with staff trained in ACLS/BLS.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which supplies are needed for a treadmill stress test? (Best answer)
options: Electrodes, skin prep, ECG stress system, BP cuff/sphygmomanometer and emergency equipment
questions.explanation: Exercise testing requires continuous multi-lead ECG monitoring, blood pressure measurement and emergency readiness.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: During exercise testing, limb electrodes are usually placed:
options: On the torso (Mason-Likar modification) to reduce motion artifact
questions.explanation: Mason-Likar placement moves limb electrodes to the shoulders/infraclavicular area and lower abdomen/hips. This changes the tracing slightly, so the resting baseline is recorded in the same position.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Why is a supine and standing resting ECG often recorded before exercise?
options: To establish a baseline in the exercise position because posture and torso leads can change the ECG
To warm up the treadmill belt
questions.explanation: Baseline tracings in the positions used allow true exercise changes to be distinguished from positional changes.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Securing lead wires with a belt, vest or tape during a treadmill test helps to:
options: Reduce motion artifact from swinging wires
questions.explanation: Stabilizing cables minimizes artifact during walking/running. Securing wires has no effect on heart rate, treadmill calibration or blood pressure.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which two modalities are commonly used for exercise stress testing in the United States?
questions.explanation: Treadmills are most common in the U.S.; cycle ergometers are useful for patients with gait or balance problems and in research.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Compared with a treadmill, a cycle ergometer usually produces:
options: A higher peak VO2 in most patients
A lower peak oxygen uptake (about 10–20% lower) because of local leg fatigue
questions.explanation: Smaller muscle mass on the bike often limits exercise before maximal cardiovascular effort.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Cycle ergometer workload is measured in:
questions.explanation: Bike workload is set in watts; treadmill workload by speed and grade. Miles per hour and % grade describe treadmill workload; millivolts measure ECG amplitude.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Holding onto the treadmill handrails tightly during the test will:
options: Reduce the oxygen cost of exercise, overestimating functional capacity, and add artifact
questions.explanation: Heavy handrail support lowers the true work performed; patients should hold lightly for balance only.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Before starting the treadmill, the technician should demonstrate:
options: How to run at full speed
How to step on and off, walk upright, and use the rails only for balance
How to stop the machine with their feet
questions.explanation: Teaching safe technique prevents falls and artifact. Patients should never be taught to run at full speed, disconnect the ECG, or stop the belt with their feet.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The treadmill emergency stop should be:
options: Known, accessible and tested before the patient begins
Used to end every normal test abruptly
Covered so the patient cannot press it
questions.explanation: Staff must be able to stop the belt immediately in an emergency. Covering or disabling it is unsafe, and normal tests end with a gradual cool-down, not an abrupt stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: One MET (metabolic equivalent) is defined as about:
options: 3.5 mL O2 per kg per minute (resting oxygen consumption)
questions.explanation: 1 MET ≈ resting energy expenditure; workloads are expressed as multiples of rest. 10 and 35 mL/kg/min are multiples of rest (≈3 and 10 METs); 1 L/min is an absolute VO2, not a MET.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Functional capacity is commonly reported in:
questions.explanation: Exercise capacity in METs is a strong prognostic marker. Millivolts, small boxes and joules describe ECG amplitude, time and defibrillation energy.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The most widely used treadmill protocol is the:
questions.explanation: The Bruce protocol is the standard clinical treadmill protocol in the U.S. Naughton and Balke are lower-intensity alternatives; "Lewis" is a lead, not a protocol.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Each stage of the standard Bruce protocol lasts:
questions.explanation: Bruce stages are 3 minutes, increasing speed and grade each stage. 1- and 2-minute stages are used by other protocols (e.g., ramp, Naughton); Bruce does not use 5-minute stages.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Stage 1 of the standard Bruce protocol is:
questions.explanation: Bruce: Stage 1 1.7 mph/10%; Stage 2 2.5 mph/12%; Stage 3 3.4 mph/14%; Stage 4 4.2 mph/16%; Stage 5 5.0 mph/18%.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Stage 2 of the Bruce protocol is:
questions.explanation: Stage 2 = 2.5 mph, 12% grade. 1.7/10 is stage 1, 3.4/14 is stage 3, and 2.0/3.5 is a Naughton-type workload.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Stage 3 of the Bruce protocol is:
questions.explanation: Stage 3 = 3.4 mph, 14% grade. 4.2/16 is stage 4 and 2.5/12 is stage 2.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Stage 4 of the Bruce protocol is:
questions.explanation: Stage 4 = 4.2 mph, 16% grade; stage 5 = 5.0 mph, 18%. 5.0/18 is stage 5 and 3.4/14 is stage 3.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Put the first four standard Bruce stages in order (speed/grade).
questions.explanation: Bruce increases both speed and grade every 3 minutes: 1.7/10 → 2.5/12 → 3.4/14 → 4.2/16 → 5.0/18.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The Modified Bruce protocol differs from the standard Bruce by:
options: Adding two lower-workload stages at 1.7 mph (0% then 5% grade) before standard Stage 1
questions.explanation: Modified Bruce begins with 1.7 mph/0% and 1.7 mph/5% (3 min each) for elderly, deconditioned or post-MI patients.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The Naughton protocol is best suited for:
options: Patients with limited exercise capacity (e.g., heart failure, elderly), using small workload increments
questions.explanation: Naughton uses slow speeds and small grade increases (about 1 MET per stage) in 2-minute stages.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Ideally, the exercise protocol should be chosen so that the patient reaches maximal effort in about:
questions.explanation: An individualized protocol that ends in 8–12 minutes provides the best estimate of functional capacity.
questions.source: Gibbons et al., ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing

questions.stem: Age-predicted maximal heart rate (APMHR) is commonly estimated as:
questions.explanation: The traditional estimate is 220 − age (other formulas exist, e.g., 208 − 0.7 × age). 200 − age, 220 + age and 180 − age are not the standard formula.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A "target" or adequate heart rate for a diagnostic exercise test is commonly at least:
questions.explanation: Reaching ≥85% of APMHR is commonly used to define an adequate (diagnostic) test. 50% is far too low to be diagnostic and 110% exceeds the predicted maximum.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: During exercise, blood pressure is normally measured:
options: At rest, during each stage (usually the last minute), at peak exercise and during recovery
questions.explanation: Regular BP monitoring identifies abnormal responses such as exercise-induced hypotension. Measuring only before or after misses exercise hypotension or hypertensive responses; every 10 seconds is impractical.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The normal systolic blood pressure response to dynamic exercise is to:
questions.explanation: SBP rises with workload (roughly 10 mm Hg per MET); diastolic changes little or falls slightly. A drop in SBP with increasing workload is abnormal.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Recovery monitoring after exercise usually continues for at least:
options: 5–6 minutes, or longer until ECG, BP and symptoms return near baseline
questions.explanation: Many ischemic changes and arrhythmias appear in recovery; monitoring continues until the patient is stable.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: An exercise ECG is considered "positive" for ischemia when there is:
options: ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping ST depression, measured 60–80 ms after the J point
Any upsloping ST depression of 0.5 mm
questions.explanation: The standard criterion is ≥1 mm (0.1 mV) horizontal or downsloping ST depression at 60–80 ms after J.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Rapidly upsloping ST depression at peak exercise that returns to baseline within 80 ms of the J point is usually:
questions.explanation: J-point depression with rapid upsloping ST is common in normal subjects. Positive tests require horizontal or downsloping depression; STEMI requires ST elevation.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Put the stress test sequence in order.
items: Verify order, identify patient and obtain informed consent
Record resting ECG and blood pressure (supine and standing)
Begin exercise protocol with continuous monitoring
Stop exercise at endpoint and begin recovery
Monitor recovery until stable, then remove electrodes
questions.explanation: Consent and prep → baseline ECG/BP → graded exercise with monitoring → endpoint → monitored recovery.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Using 220 − age, a 50-year-old's 85% target heart rate is:
questions.explanation: 220 − 50 = 170; 170 × 0.85 = 144.5 ≈ 145 bpm. 170 is the full predicted maximum; 128 and 153 use the wrong percentage.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which are ABSOLUTE contraindications to exercise testing? (Select three.)
options: History of a remote MI 5 years ago
questions.explanation: AHA absolute contraindications include acute MI (within 2 days), ongoing unstable angina, uncontrolled symptomatic arrhythmias, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, decompensated heart failure, acute PE, acute myocarditis/pericarditis and acute aortic dissection.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to exercise stress testing?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation of the heart or pericardium is an absolute contraindication. LBBB limits ECG interpretation but is not a contraindication.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is a RELATIVE contraindication to exercise testing?
questions.explanation: Severe resting hypertension (SBP >200 and/or DBP >110) is relative; the others are absolute contraindications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is a RELATIVE contraindication to exercise testing?
options: Known left main coronary artery stenosis
questions.explanation: Known left main disease, moderate stenotic valve disease, electrolyte abnormalities, tachy/bradyarrhythmias, high-degree AV block and HCM with obstruction are relative contraindications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which resting ECG finding makes exercise ECG interpretation for ischemia unreliable, so imaging is usually added?
questions.explanation: LBBB, ventricular pacing, WPW, >1 mm resting ST depression and digoxin effect impair ST interpretation; imaging (and for LBBB, vasodilator stress) is preferred.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which are ABSOLUTE indications to stop an exercise test? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: AHA absolute indications: ST elevation >1 mm in leads without Q waves (not V1/aVR), SBP drop >10 mm Hg with other ischemia evidence, moderate-severe angina, CNS symptoms, signs of poor perfusion, sustained VT, technical inability to monitor ECG/BP, and the subject's desire to stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: During exercise, the patient develops 2 mm ST elevation in V2–V4 (no prior Q waves). The technician should:
options: Continue to reach target heart rate
Stop the test immediately (absolute indication) and alert the physician
Ignore it since it is not depression
questions.explanation: ST elevation ≥1 mm in leads without Q waves (other than V1 or aVR) is an absolute indication to terminate.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Systolic blood pressure falls from 150 to 130 mm Hg as the treadmill workload increases, and the patient has chest pain. This is:
options: Irrelevant if heart rate is rising
An absolute indication to stop the test
questions.explanation: A drop in SBP >10 mm Hg from baseline despite increasing workload with other evidence of ischemia is an absolute indication to stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is a RELATIVE indication to stop an exercise test?
options: Hypertensive response: SBP > 250 mm Hg and/or DBP > 115 mm Hg
questions.explanation: A hypertensive response is a relative indication. Sustained VT, patient request and CNS symptoms are absolute.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which arrhythmia is listed as a RELATIVE (not absolute) indication to terminate exercise?
questions.explanation: Arrhythmias other than sustained VT (multifocal PVCs, triplets, SVT, heart block, bradyarrhythmias) are relative indications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: > 2 mm horizontal or downsloping ST depression during exercise is classified by AHA as:
questions.explanation: Marked ST depression (>2 mm horizontal/downsloping) is a relative indication; ST elevation without Q waves is absolute.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The patient becomes ataxic and dizzy, nearly fainting, at stage 3. You should:
options: Encourage them to finish the stage
Leave to get the physician first
Stop exercise immediately, support the patient, lay them down and alert the physician
questions.explanation: Central nervous system symptoms (ataxia, dizziness, near-syncope) are absolute indications to stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: New development of bundle branch block during exercise that cannot be distinguished from VT is:
options: An absolute indication to increase workload
questions.explanation: Exercise-induced BBB or IVCD that cannot be distinguished from VT is listed as a relative indication.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: If the ECG signal becomes unreadable because of artifact during exercise, the test should be:
options: Stopped—technical difficulty monitoring ECG or BP is an absolute indication
Continued as long as the patient feels fine
questions.explanation: Inability to monitor the ECG or blood pressure safely is an absolute indication to stop. Continuing without a readable ECG or BP is unsafe, and a Holter cannot replace stress monitoring.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: At peak exercise the patient's heart rate is 168 and they report severe fatigue and shortness of breath; ECG is unchanged. This is:
options: Not a reason to stop ever
A relative indication; the physician may stop the test as a symptom-limited endpoint
questions.explanation: Fatigue, shortness of breath, wheezing, leg cramps or claudication are relative indications; most tests end at symptom-limited exhaustion.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Signs of poor perfusion during exercise (pallor, cyanosis, cold clammy skin) are:
options: A sign to increase the grade
questions.explanation: Signs of poor perfusion are absolute indications to terminate. Pallor and cyanosis are never a normal response, and they are absolute (not relative) indications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: After stopping for a serious endpoint, the patient should generally be placed:
options: Supine (or seated if dyspneic) for immediate monitored recovery
questions.explanation: Supine positioning maximizes venous return and allows rapid response; dyspneic patients may sit.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The most common reason a symptom-limited treadmill test ends is:
questions.explanation: Most tests end with the patient reaching maximal or near-maximal effort and fatigue. VF and equipment failure are rare; tests most often end at maximal effort.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which agents are pharmacologic VASODILATOR stress agents? (Best answer)
questions.explanation: Vasodilators cause coronary hyperemia; regions supplied by stenosed arteries show less flow on perfusion imaging.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Dobutamine stress works mainly by:
options: Increasing heart rate and contractility (beta-1 stimulation), increasing oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is an inotrope/chronotrope that simulates exercise demand; atropine may be added to reach target heart rate.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Which drug reverses persistent side effects of adenosine, regadenoson or dipyridamole?
questions.explanation: Aminophylline is an adenosine-receptor antagonist used to reverse vasodilator side effects such as bronchospasm or persistent AV block.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Which beverage must be held before an adenosine or regadenoson stress test?
options: Caffeinated drinks (coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks)
questions.explanation: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and can cause a false-negative test; usually held 12–24 hours.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: A patient with severe asthma and active wheezing is scheduled for adenosine stress. The concern is:
options: Adenosine can cause bronchospasm; the physician may choose dobutamine instead
Adenosine is contraindicated only in children
questions.explanation: Active bronchospasm is a contraindication to vasodilator stress agents; dobutamine is an alternative.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Transient AV block during adenosine infusion occurs because adenosine:
options: Increases calcium in the SA node
Blocks sodium channels in the ventricles
Slows conduction through the AV node
questions.explanation: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, often causing brief first- or second-degree block during infusion.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: In nuclear stress testing, the radioactive tracer (e.g., technetium-99m sestamibi) shows:
options: Myocardial perfusion (blood flow) at rest and stress
questions.explanation: Perfusion tracers distribute in proportion to blood flow; a defect at stress that improves at rest suggests ischemia.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: A perfusion defect present on stress images that normalizes on rest images is called:
questions.explanation: Reversible defects indicate ischemia; fixed defects suggest infarction (or attenuation artifact).
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: During an exercise nuclear test, the tracer is injected:
options: At or near peak exercise, and exercise continues about 1 minute afterward
questions.explanation: Injection near peak exercise captures maximal-stress perfusion; continued exercise lets the tracer distribute.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Dobutamine side effects such as severe tachyarrhythmia or ischemia are reversed with:
options: A short-acting beta blocker (e.g., esmolol or metoprolol) per physician order
questions.explanation: Beta blockade counters dobutamine's beta-1 effects. Aminophylline reverses vasodilators, not dobutamine; more dobutamine or caffeine would worsen the problem.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Common, usually benign side effects of adenosine include:
options: Flushing, chest pressure, shortness of breath and headache
questions.explanation: Adenosine has a very short half-life (seconds), so side effects resolve quickly once the infusion stops.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Regadenoson is given as:
options: A single fixed-dose IV bolus (0.4 mg) followed by a saline flush
questions.explanation: Regadenoson is a selective A2A agonist given as a 0.4 mg rapid IV injection; tracer is injected after the saline flush.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Stress echocardiography detects ischemia primarily by:
questions.explanation: Ischemic segments contract poorly under stress, visible on echo images. Tracer uptake is nuclear imaging; pacing spikes and QT shortening are not stress-echo endpoints.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Patients unable to exercise adequately are usually evaluated with:
questions.explanation: Pharmacologic stress with imaging is the standard alternative for those who cannot exercise.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: Why might a physician order beta blockers to be held before a diagnostic exercise test?
options: Beta blockers blunt the heart-rate response, which can prevent reaching target heart rate and reduce sensitivity
They increase the heart rate excessively
questions.explanation: Beta blockade lowers peak heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand; holding them is a physician decision.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: In recovery, the patient suddenly becomes unresponsive and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. The first action is to:
options: Call for help (code) and begin CPR/defibrillation per ACLS
questions.explanation: VF is cardiac arrest: immediate defibrillation with high-quality CPR saves lives. Recording a 12-lead or checking BP first delays defibrillation, and restarting the treadmill is never appropriate.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: A patient reports mild chest tightness at stage 2 with no ECG changes. Best action?
options: Ask them to rate the pain, inform the physician, and closely monitor ECG and BP
Tell them to hold their breath
questions.explanation: Use an angina scale; moderate-to-severe angina is an absolute stopping indication, and the physician decides based on the overall picture.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Perceived exertion during exercise is commonly rated using the:
questions.explanation: The Borg RPE scale (6–20 or 0–10) quantifies effort and helps judge maximal effort. The Glasgow Coma Scale measures consciousness, Apgar rates newborns, and there is no "Bruce index" for exertion.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which instruction is appropriate immediately after an exercise test?
options: Eat a large meal right away
Avoid a very hot shower or bath for a period after the test
questions.explanation: Hot showers soon after exercise can cause vasodilation and hypotension; many labs advise waiting.
questions.source: Gibbons et al., ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing

questions.stem: A diabetic patient becomes shaky and sweaty before the test, having skipped breakfast. You should:
options: Check with the nurse/physician—possible hypoglycemia—before starting
Ignore it because it is nerves
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia symptoms can mimic anxiety; follow protocol for glucose check and physician direction.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: If chest pain occurs during the test, the physician may use which standardized scale?
questions.explanation: Angina scales grade chest pain severity during exercise; grade 3–4 (moderate-severe) is an absolute indication to stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The physician supervising a stress test must be:
options: Immediately available per facility policy and trained in emergency cardiac care
questions.explanation: Supervision requirements vary, but a qualified provider must be immediately available, and staff must be ACLS/BLS trained.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A Holter monitor continuously records the ECG typically for:
questions.explanation: Holters record every beat continuously, usually for 24–48 hours (some newer patch devices record longer).
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: The main purpose of a Holter monitor is to:
options: Correlate symptoms with heart rhythm and detect arrhythmias during normal daily activities
questions.explanation: Ambulatory ECG captures rhythm during everyday life and links it to diary-recorded symptoms.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: An event (loop) recorder differs from a Holter because it:
options: Is worn for weeks and stores ECG around patient-activated or automatically detected events
questions.explanation: Event/loop recorders monitor for longer periods (often up to 30 days) to catch infrequent symptoms.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: An implantable loop recorder (ILR) is best for:
options: Very infrequent symptoms such as unexplained syncope, monitoring for up to about 3 years
questions.explanation: ILRs are inserted under the skin and can monitor for years. A 24-hour rhythm check needs a Holter, exercise testing uses a treadmill, and QT is measured on a 12-lead.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Mobile cardiac telemetry (MCT/MCOT) differs from a standard event monitor because it:
options: Automatically transmits detected arrhythmias to a monitoring center in near real time
questions.explanation: MCT continuously analyzes the ECG and sends events for prompt review. MCT has ECG electrodes, records rhythm (not blood pressure) and is used outside the hospital.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: In-hospital telemetry primarily allows:
options: Continuous remote rhythm surveillance by trained monitor watchers
questions.explanation: Telemetry transmits the ECG to a central station for continuous observation of hospitalized patients.
questions.source: Drew et al., AHA Practice Standards for Electrocardiographic Monitoring in Hospital Settings (Circulation 2004; update 2017)

questions.stem: The patient diary is important because it:
options: Lets the reader correlate symptoms and activities with the recorded rhythm at the same time
questions.explanation: Symptom–rhythm correlation is the key diagnostic goal of ambulatory monitoring. The diary does not replace the recording, measure heart rate, or exist for billing.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Patients should mark the diary and/or press the event button when they:
options: Feel symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness or chest pain
questions.explanation: Event marking time-stamps the symptomatic periods for analysis. Meals and routine activities are logged in the diary, but the event button is for symptoms.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Before applying a Holter, the technician should check:
options: That the BP cuff is inflated
That the defibrillator pads are on
Fresh battery/charged device, correct time and date, and functioning lead wires
questions.explanation: Pre-application checks ensure a full-length recording with correct time stamps. Treadmills, BP cuffs and defibrillator pads are not part of a Holter hook-up.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Why must the Holter recorder's clock be set accurately?
options: So the diary times match the recorded ECG times
questions.explanation: Incorrect time makes symptom–rhythm correlation unreliable. The clock does not change print speed, paper speed or QTc.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: After application, the technician verifies the signal by:
options: Viewing the ECG on the recorder or hook-up device for clear tracings in each channel before the patient leaves
questions.explanation: Verifying signal quality before release prevents unusable recordings. Assuming it works or waiting for the report risks an unusable 24-hour recording.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: When the Holter is returned, the technician should:
options: Check that the recording is complete, retrieve the diary and clean/disinfect the device
Reuse electrodes on the next patient
questions.explanation: Post-use checks confirm data integrity and prepare the equipment safely for the next patient.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Most traditional Holter monitors record how many channels?
questions.explanation: Conventional Holters record 2–3 channels using 5 or 7 electrodes; 12-lead Holters exist. Most Holters are not 12-channel or 24-channel, and single-channel devices are patches or event monitors.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Holter electrodes are usually placed:
options: On the abdomen over soft tissue
On the chest over bone (sternum and ribs), avoiding large muscles
questions.explanation: Placing electrodes over bony areas of the torso reduces muscle and motion artifact during daily activities.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Skin preparation for a Holter is especially important because:
options: The recording lasts many hours during movement, so low impedance and good adhesion are needed
questions.explanation: Thorough cleaning, drying, hair removal and light abrasion improve long-term signal quality.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Creating a stress loop (strain-relief loop) in the lead wires and taping it helps to:
options: Prevent tugging that pulls electrodes and causes artifact
questions.explanation: Loops absorb movement so the electrode stays in place. (CCI lists "stress loops, pouch" in the ambulatory task list.)
questions.source: CCI CCT examination matrix & task list (cci-online.org)

questions.stem: Put the Holter hook-up steps in order.
items: Verify order and identify the patient
Apply electrodes and connect lead wires with stress loops
Insert battery/start recorder and verify signal
Secure the recorder in its pouch and give final instructions
questions.explanation: Order/ID → education → skin prep → electrodes with strain relief → start and verify → secure and instruct.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: The Holter recorder is carried:
options: In a pouch on a belt or shoulder strap, secured to avoid pulling
Loose in a pocket with wires dangling
questions.explanation: A secure pouch prevents strain on the leads. Dangling wires pull electrodes; a recorder must never get wet or be taped to the electrodes.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Which instructions should a Holter patient receive? (Select three.)
options: Keep the recorder dry—no bathing or swimming
Sleep with an electric blanket on the recorder
Record symptoms and activities with times in the diary
questions.explanation: Patients keep the device dry, carry on with normal life (so typical symptoms occur) and keep a detailed diary.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Why should a Holter patient avoid electric blankets and strong magnets/metal detectors when possible?
options: They can cause electrical interference with the recording
questions.explanation: Strong electromagnetic sources can create artifact. These devices do not change the heart rate or improve the signal.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A patient asks whether they can exercise while wearing a Holter. The best answer is:
options: "Run as fast as possible to cause symptoms."
"Yes—do your usual activities and note them in your diary."
questions.explanation: Normal activity is encouraged; recording activities helps interpret heart-rate changes. Restricting activity or removing the monitor defeats the purpose; deliberately provoking symptoms is unsafe.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: If an electrode comes loose at home, the patient should be told to:
options: Press it back on or replace it as instructed and note the time in the diary
Tape it to a different body part
questions.explanation: Simple instructions for re-securing electrodes preserve the recording. Removing the monitor or ignoring the loose electrode loses data; electrodes go only on the prepared chest sites.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A patient wearing an event monitor feels palpitations. They should:
options: Wait for the symptoms to end
Activate the recording button and note symptoms, then transmit per instructions
questions.explanation: Patient activation captures the event; severe symptoms (chest pain, fainting) warrant emergency care.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A patient wearing a Holter develops crushing chest pain at home. They should be instructed to:
options: Press the event button and wait
Remove the Holter and go to sleep
Write it down and return the next day
Call emergency services (911) immediately; the monitor is not an alarm system
questions.explanation: Holters do not alert anyone in real time; emergencies require calling 911. Pressing the event button, waiting or going to sleep delays emergency care.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A Holter recording has long periods of flat line in one channel. The most likely cause is:
options: A loose electrode or broken lead wire on that channel
questions.explanation: A channel-specific flat line is technical. Asystole would appear in all channels and with symptoms.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A Holter report shows only 6 hours of recording instead of 24. A likely cause is:
options: A depleted battery or memory problem, or the device was removed early
questions.explanation: Battery and device checks before hook-up prevent short recordings. Slow rates or AF do not shorten the recording.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Intermittent bursts of high-frequency noise while the patient was gardening are most likely:
questions.explanation: Activity-related noise during arm exercise is artifact; check the diary and other channels.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Motion artifact on a Holter can mimic which arrhythmia most commonly?
questions.explanation: Rhythmic motion (e.g., brushing teeth) can resemble VT; look for normal QRS complexes "marching through" the artifact.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Telemetry alarms "leads off" repeatedly. The first step is to:
options: Check the patient and the electrode/lead connections
questions.explanation: Assess the patient first, then fix electrode contact; never disable alarms. Silencing alarms, raising gain or removing the monitor ignores a possible patient problem.
questions.source: Drew et al., AHA Practice Standards for Electrocardiographic Monitoring in Hospital Settings (Circulation 2004; update 2017)

questions.stem: A Holter channel shows a wandering baseline every few seconds. The most likely cause is:
options: Poor skin prep or an electrode moving with respiration
questions.explanation: Baseline wander comes from impedance changes with movement; better skin prep and strain relief help.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: The patient's diary says "dizzy at 2:15 pm," but the recording shows normal sinus rhythm at that time. This means:
options: The test must be repeated always
The symptom did not correlate with an arrhythmia at that moment—useful diagnostic information
questions.explanation: A symptom without arrhythmia (negative correlation) helps rule out a rhythm cause for that symptom.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A patient with a pacemaker is getting a Holter. The technician should:
options: Note the pacemaker on the requisition and enable pacemaker detection if available
questions.explanation: Pacemaker information helps the analyst evaluate pacing function. Technicians never turn off pacemakers, refuse the test, or edit data.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Holter reports commonly include:
options: Minimum, maximum and average heart rate, ectopic beat counts, pauses and arrhythmia episodes
questions.explanation: Summary statistics plus representative strips form the Holter report. Ejection fraction and valve areas come from echocardiography; cholesterol comes from blood tests.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: During sleep on a Holter, which finding is commonly normal?
questions.explanation: Heart rates normally fall during sleep; brief sinus bradycardia is expected. VT, complete heart block and 10-second asystole are abnormal at any time.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Heart rate variability (HRV) analysis from Holter data reflects:
questions.explanation: HRV measures beat-to-beat variation and is a marker of autonomic tone. HRV does not show coronary anatomy, valve function or electrode quality.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Holter monitoring can help evaluate pacemaker function by:
options: Showing pacing, capture and sensing over a full day of activities
questions.explanation: Holter recordings can reveal intermittent failure to capture or sense; device interrogation remains definitive.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A pause greater than about ___ seconds while awake is commonly flagged as significant on Holter reports.
questions.explanation: Pauses ≥3 seconds are commonly reported as clinically significant (thresholds vary by lab and clinical context).
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: Which monitor is best for a patient with daily palpitations?
questions.explanation: Daily symptoms are likely to occur during a 24–48 hour Holter; rarer symptoms need longer monitoring.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Which monitor is best for symptoms that occur about once every two weeks?
options: An external event/loop recorder or mobile telemetry for up to 30 days
questions.explanation: Monitoring duration should match symptom frequency. A 24-hour Holter or resting ECG would likely miss a symptom that occurs every two weeks; a stress test only covers exercise.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A patch ECG monitor is:
options: A single-lead adhesive device worn on the chest for days to weeks
questions.explanation: Patch monitors are leadless, water-resistant and record continuously for up to about 14 days (device dependent).
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: For a Holter, the patient's chest should NOT be:
options: Covered with lotion or oil at the electrode sites
questions.explanation: Lotion prevents adhesion over the long recording. Cleaning, drying and light abrasion are all correct prep steps.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: The normal PR interval in adults is:
questions.explanation: PR 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes). Longer = first-degree AV block; shorter can mean junctional rhythm or pre-excitation.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A normal QRS duration in adults is:
questions.explanation: Narrow QRS (<0.12 s) means ventricles were activated through the normal conduction system.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The PR interval is measured from:
options: The end of the P wave to the end of the QRS
The beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex
The beginning of the QRS to the end of the T wave
The peak of the P wave to the peak of the R wave
questions.explanation: PR = start of P → start of QRS (whether it starts with a Q or R wave). The other options describe parts of the P wave, R-wave peaks or the QT interval.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The QT interval is measured from:
options: The peak of the R wave to the peak of the T wave
The end of the QRS to the start of the T wave
The beginning of the QRS to the end of the T wave
The start of the P wave to the end of the T wave
questions.explanation: QT includes ventricular depolarization and repolarization; it shortens with faster rates, hence QTc.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The ST segment is the portion between the:
options: End of the P wave and start of the QRS
Start of the QRS and end of the T wave
J point (end of QRS) and the beginning of the T wave
End of the T wave and next P wave
questions.explanation: The ST segment is normally isoelectric; elevation or depression may signal injury or ischemia.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A small rounded wave sometimes seen after the T wave, best in V2–V3, is the:
questions.explanation: U waves are often normal and small; prominent U waves suggest hypokalemia. Delta waves are part of the QRS upstroke in WPW, Osborn waves are J-point waves in hypothermia, and F waves are flutter waves.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A PR interval of 0.28 s that is the same for every beat, with every P followed by a QRS, is:
questions.explanation: First-degree block is simply a prolonged, constant PR (>0.20 s) with 1:1 conduction. Mobitz I lengthens the PR until a beat drops, Mobitz II and third-degree block have non-conducted P waves.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which interval best reflects the time of ventricular depolarization only?
questions.explanation: QRS duration = ventricular depolarization. QT = depolarization + repolarization.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: A prolonged QT interval predisposes the patient to:
questions.explanation: Long QT (congenital, drugs, low K/Mg) increases risk of polymorphic VT—torsades. Flutter, sinus tachycardia and wandering atrial pacemaker are not caused by a long QT.
questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: An "inverted P wave before a narrow QRS with a PR < 0.12 s" in lead II suggests the impulse originated in the:
questions.explanation: Retrograde atrial activation from the junction produces negative P waves in II, III, aVF with a short PR (or P hidden/after QRS).
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which waveform is "hidden" within the QRS in a normal ECG?
questions.explanation: Atrial repolarization coincides with ventricular depolarization and is usually not seen. Ventricular depolarization is the QRS itself; P and U waves are visible outside it.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using the 300 method, if there are 4 large boxes between R waves, the heart rate is:
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using the 1,500 method, 20 small boxes between R waves equals a rate of:
questions.explanation: 1500 ÷ 20 = 75 bpm. The 1,500 method is the most precise for regular rhythms.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which method is best for estimating rate in an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation?
options: 300 ÷ large boxes between two R waves
1,500 ÷ small boxes between two R waves
Count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
questions.explanation: The 6-second method averages beats over time; R–R methods assume regularity. The 300 and 1,500 methods and single R–R measurements give misleading rates when R–R intervals vary.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using the 300 method, one large box between R waves indicates a rate of:
questions.explanation: 300 ÷ 1 = 300 bpm (e.g., atrial flutter waves); 2 boxes = 150 bpm. 150 bpm is two boxes, 100 is three, and 30 would be ten boxes.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Seven QRS complexes appear in a 6-second strip. The approximate rate is:
questions.explanation: 7 × 10 = 70 bpm. 42 would be 7 × 6; 60 would need 6 complexes; 7 bpm is the raw count, not the rate.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: An R–R interval measures 0.60 s. The heart rate is:
questions.explanation: Rate = 60 ÷ R–R (s) = 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100 bpm. Equivalent: 15 small boxes → 1500/15 = 100.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which rhythms are pulseless cardiac arrest rhythms that may require defibrillation? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: VF and pulseless VT are "shockable." Asystole and PEA are arrest rhythms but are not shockable—treat with CPR and epinephrine.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Asystole is treated with:
questions.explanation: Asystole is non-shockable; confirm in more than one lead and check leads/gain. Defibrillation and synchronized cardioversion need organized or fibrillating electrical activity; adenosine treats SVT.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Before calling a rhythm asystole, the technician should:
options: Confirm in a second lead and check that leads are connected and gain is adequate
questions.explanation: Fine VF or a disconnected lead can look like a flat line. Shocking a flat line is not indicated, and waiting delays CPR.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) means:
options: An organized rhythm is seen on the monitor but there is no palpable pulse
A normal rhythm with a strong pulse
questions.explanation: PEA is diagnosed clinically: organized electrical activity without mechanical output. No electrical activity is asystole; VF never has a pulse; a strong pulse rules out PEA.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: The technician sees sustained VT on a monitor. The first step is to:
options: Wait to see if it stops
Print the strip and file it
Check the patient for responsiveness and a pulse, and call for help
questions.explanation: Assess the patient; pulseless VT is arrest (CPR/defibrillation), while VT with a pulse needs urgent physician management.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Which rhythm is MOST immediately life-threatening?
