questions.explanation: VF produces no cardiac output and is fatal within minutes without defibrillation. First-degree block, sinus arrhythmia and PACs are usually benign.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Why is Mobitz II second-degree AV block considered more dangerous than Mobitz I?
options: It usually reflects disease below the AV node and can progress suddenly to complete heart block
It has a narrow QRS in every case
It is always caused by athletes' training
questions.explanation: Mobitz II is infranodal and unpredictable; pacing is often indicated. Mobitz I is usually AV nodal and more benign.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: A technician recording a routine ECG notices third-degree AV block at a rate of 32. The technician should:
options: Immediately notify the nurse/physician per critical-result policy and stay with the patient
Tell the patient they need a pacemaker
Place the ECG in the routine stack
questions.explanation: Critical rhythms are reported immediately; diagnosis and plans are discussed with the patient by the provider.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: When reporting a rhythm strip, which information should be included?
options: Patient identifiers, date/time, lead, rate, regularity, intervals and the rhythm observed
questions.explanation: A complete description lets the reader verify the interpretation. A rhythm name alone or a room number is incomplete, and treatment opinions are outside the technician's role.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Telling a patient "you are having a heart attack" based on your ECG is:
options: Outside the technician's scope of practice
questions.explanation: Technicians report findings to providers; diagnosis is communicated by the provider. No law requires it and it is not part of consent; diagnosis is the provider's role.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A clear way to communicate a critical finding to a nurse by phone is:
options: Text a photo to your personal phone
Identify yourself and the patient, state the finding, and have the receiver read it back
questions.explanation: Closed-loop communication (e.g., SBAR with read-back) reduces errors. Voicemails, personal-phone photos (HIPAA) and waiting for rounds delay or endanger care.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: Rhythm strips mounted in the chart must be labeled with:
options: Patient name/ID, date, time and lead
questions.explanation: Labels make strips traceable and comparable. A date or initials alone cannot link a strip to the right patient and time.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: In the NBG pacemaker code "VVI," the first letter indicates:
questions.explanation: Position 1 = chamber paced; 2 = chamber sensed; 3 = response to sensing (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = dual); 4 = rate modulation (R).
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: A "DDD" pacemaker:
options: Paces only at a fixed rate
Paces and senses both atria and ventricles, with dual (inhibited and triggered) response
questions.explanation: DDD = dual chamber paced, dual sensed, dual response; it maintains AV synchrony. Atrial-only pacing is AAI; no sensing is asynchronous (e.g., DOO); fixed-rate pacing is not DDD behavior.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: A pacing spike followed by a wide QRS complex indicates:
questions.explanation: A ventricular-paced beat produces a wide QRS (LBBB-like from RV apex) right after the spike.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: Pacing spikes appear without a following P wave or QRS complex. This is:
questions.explanation: The pacemaker fired but the myocardium did not depolarize (e.g., lead displacement, high threshold).
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: Pacing spikes occur on or right after the patient's own QRS complexes or T waves. This is:
questions.explanation: The pacemaker did not "see" the intrinsic beat and fired anyway; a spike on the T wave can trigger VT/VF.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: The heart rate falls below the programmed lower rate and no pacing spikes appear, while the patient's own rhythm pauses. A likely explanation is:
options: Oversensing (the pacemaker is inhibited by signals it should ignore) or failure to pace
questions.explanation: Inappropriate inhibition from muscle noise or T waves (oversensing), or output failure, produces pauses without spikes.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: A magnet placed over most pacemakers causes:
options: Asynchronous (fixed-rate) pacing for as long as the magnet is applied
questions.explanation: Magnet mode tests output/battery; effects vary by device and ICD magnets suspend tachy therapy instead.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes artifact from a true arrhythmia?
options: The artifact is always wider than 0.12 s
Artifact never appears in lead II
Normal QRS complexes can be seen "marching through" the disturbance at the expected intervals
questions.explanation: If the underlying QRS complexes continue on schedule, the chaotic baseline is artifact, not VF/VT.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Somatic tremor artifact can be mistaken for:
questions.explanation: Regular tremors (e.g., Parkinson ~4–6 Hz) may mimic flutter waves; irregular tremor may mimic fibrillatory waves.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Beta blockers such as metoprolol typically cause:
options: Slower heart rate and slower AV conduction (longer PR)
questions.explanation: Beta blockers block sympathetic beta-1 effects, slowing the SA node and AV node (class II antiarrhythmic).
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Medications ending in "-olol" (e.g., atenolol, metoprolol, propranolol) belong to which class?
questions.explanation: Generic suffixes: -olol beta blockers; -pril ACE inhibitors; -sartan ARBs; -dipine dihydropyridine CCBs.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Medications ending in "-pril" (e.g., lisinopril, enalapril) are:
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure and reduce cardiac remodeling; common side effects include dry cough and hyperkalemia.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: A common side effect of ACE inhibitors is:
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, causing cough; angioedema is rare but serious. They can also raise potassium.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Drugs ending in "-sartan" (e.g., losartan, valsartan) are:
questions.explanation: ARBs block angiotensin II receptors; they lower BP without the ACE-inhibitor cough. Beta blockers end in -olol; loop diuretics include furosemide; nitrates include nitroglycerin.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Diltiazem and verapamil (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) affect the ECG by:
options: Slowing AV-node conduction and heart rate
questions.explanation: Class IV antiarrhythmics slow the SA/AV nodes; used for rate control in AF/flutter and SVT.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: In the Vaughan Williams classification, amiodarone is primarily a class:
questions.explanation: Class III drugs (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide) prolong repolarization and the QT interval. Amiodarone also has class I, II and IV actions.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Which ECG effect is expected with class III antiarrhythmics such as sotalol or amiodarone?
questions.explanation: Prolonged repolarization lengthens QT; excessive QT prolongation risks torsades. QT shortening, peaked T waves and a short PR are not class III effects.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Class I antiarrhythmics such as flecainide and procainamide primarily:
options: Block calcium channels in the AV node only
Block sodium channels and can widen the QRS
questions.explanation: Sodium channel blockade slows conduction; QRS widening is a sign of effect or toxicity. Beta blockade is class II, calcium-channel blockade class IV, and diuretics are not antiarrhythmics.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Adenosine is used to:
options: Terminate (or reveal) SVT by briefly blocking the AV node
questions.explanation: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds; a transient pause or asystole after the dose is expected.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Atropine is the first-line drug for:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks vagal tone, increasing SA-node rate and AV conduction (AHA bradycardia algorithm).
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Epinephrine during cardiac arrest is given mainly to:
options: Increase coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure through vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes is used in all arrest rhythms (VF/pVT after defibrillation, asystole/PEA).
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Digoxin toxicity can cause:
options: Almost any arrhythmia, including PAT with block, AV block and PVCs/bidirectional VT
questions.explanation: Digoxin increases automaticity and slows AV conduction; toxicity is worsened by hypokalemia. Nausea and visual changes (yellow-green halos) are classic symptoms.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Nitroglycerin relieves angina mainly by:
options: Vasodilation, which reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Nitrates dilate veins (and coronary arteries); headache and hypotension are common side effects.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Nitroglycerin should be avoided in a patient who recently took sildenafil (Viagra) because:
options: The combination can cause severe hypotension
questions.explanation: PDE-5 inhibitors plus nitrates produce dangerous blood pressure drops. The combination lowers—not raises—blood pressure and does not affect potassium or AV conduction.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Loop diuretics such as furosemide can lead to which ECG change through electrolyte loss?
options: Flattened T waves and U waves from hypokalemia
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics waste potassium and magnesium, which also increases arrhythmia risk. Peaked T waves indicate hyperkalemia; delta waves indicate WPW; short QT indicates hypercalcemia.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Warfarin, heparin and apixaban are all:
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants reduce clot formation (e.g., stroke prevention in AF). They do not change the ECG directly, but bleeding risk matters for skin prep and abrasion.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Lidocaine is a class Ib antiarrhythmic used for:
questions.explanation: Lidocaine is an alternative to amiodarone for VF/pVT in ACLS. Atrial flutter rate control uses AV-nodal blockers, bradycardia uses atropine, and hypertension uses antihypertensives.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Which medication is used for torsades de pointes?
questions.explanation: IV magnesium is first-line for torsades associated with a long QT. Adenosine treats SVT, atropine treats bradycardia, and digoxin is not used for torsades.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Which drug classes commonly slow the heart rate? (Select three.)
questions.explanation: Beta blockers, diltiazem/verapamil and digoxin slow SA/AV-node activity; atropine and epinephrine increase rate.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Two patients with the same last name are in adjacent rooms. Which practice best prevents a mix-up?
options: Ask a visitor which patient is which
Use two identifiers (full name and DOB) and match them to the order and wristband for each patient
questions.explanation: Name alerts and two-identifier checks prevent wrong-patient errors when names are similar.
questions.source: The Joint Commission, National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG.01.01.01)

questions.stem: An order says "12-lead ECG with right-sided leads" but your machine has no V4R label option. You should:
options: Record the right-sided leads and manually relabel the tracing clearly (e.g., V4R)
questions.explanation: Modified leads must be clearly labeled so the reader does not mistake them for standard positions.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A patient who speaks only Spanish is about to sign consent for a stress test. Before signing, you should:
options: Have the patient sign quickly to save time
Make sure a qualified medical interpreter explains the consent per policy
questions.explanation: Valid informed consent requires the patient to understand the information. Rushing, using a child as interpreter or skipping consent invalidates the consent process.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Gloves should be worn for an ECG when:
options: Contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin or contaminated equipment is possible (or isolation requires it)
questions.explanation: Standard precautions call for gloves when contact with potentially infectious material is anticipated; hand hygiene is still required after removing gloves.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: A patient is on neutropenic (protective) precautions. Your priority is to:
options: Protect yourself from the patient only
Avoid hand hygiene to save time
Protect the patient from your germs: hand hygiene, clean equipment and PPE per policy
questions.explanation: Immunocompromised patients need protection from infection; equipment should be cleaned before entering.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: A patient has an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). During a routine ECG you should:
options: Place a magnet over the device
Proceed normally—ECG recording does not affect the ICD—but note the device on the request
questions.explanation: Recording an ECG is safe with ICDs and pacemakers; magnets are applied only on physician direction.
questions.source: Kusumoto et al., 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

questions.stem: Which piece of personal equipment is a common electrical hazard if brought near the patient's bed by visitors?
options: An ungrounded or damaged personal electrical device plugged in near the patient
questions.explanation: Uninspected or damaged electrical devices can cause shock or interference; follow facility policy on personal equipment.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Before a resting ECG, a patient asks if they need to remove their necklace. The best response is:
options: Remove all clothing below the waist
Jewelry makes the heart rate faster
Metal jewelry usually does not affect the ECG, but move it away from electrode sites for good contact and comfort
questions.explanation: Jewelry rarely causes artifact unless it touches electrodes or wires; move items away from the sites.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which gown/positioning practice protects patient dignity during a 12-lead?
options: Leave the patient uncovered with the curtain open
Expose only the areas needed and cover the patient between steps
Ask the patient to undress fully in the hallway
questions.explanation: Privacy and draping respect dignity and reduce anxiety (and muscle artifact). Leaving the patient exposed or undressing in a hallway violates privacy and dignity.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: Before moving a patient with an IV line onto the treadmill area, you should:
options: Check that the IV line has enough slack and is secured so it will not be pulled
questions.explanation: Lines and tubes are secured before moving patients to prevent dislodgement. Technicians do not remove or clamp IVs; ignoring the line risks dislodging it.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: The midaxillary line runs vertically from the:
options: Center of the armpit (axilla) down the side of the chest
questions.explanation: Anterior axillary line = front fold of the axilla (V5); midaxillary line = center of the axilla (V6); posterior axillary line = back fold (V7).
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The midclavicular line used for V4 is found by:
options: Dropping a vertical line from the midpoint of the clavicle
Using the nipple in every patient
questions.explanation: Using the clavicle midpoint is more reliable than the nipple, which varies in position. The sternal border is V1/V2's landmark, the nipple varies between patients, and fixed distances ignore body size.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Thermal paper ECG printouts should be stored away from heat and light because:
options: They fade or darken over time and may become unreadable
questions.explanation: Thermal tracings degrade; scanned/electronic copies are kept for the record. Thermal paper does not become radioactive or change speed or calibration.
questions.source: Standard ECG textbook content (Booth & O'Brien; Dubin)

questions.stem: A resident asks you to perform a stress test on a patient whose order lists a recent MI 1 day ago. You should:
options: Give the patient nitroglycerin and proceed
Hold the test and notify the supervising physician—acute MI within 2 days is an absolute contraindication
questions.explanation: Technicians should recognize absolute contraindications and confirm with the physician before proceeding.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Precordial electrodes should be spaced so that they:
options: Are placed on top of clothing
Do not touch or overlap each other (or the gel areas)
questions.explanation: Overlapping electrodes or gel bridges create shared signals and artifact. Overlap, sternal stacking or placement over clothing cause artifact and wrong leads.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which cable connects directly to each electrode?
questions.explanation: Each lead wire clips or snaps to an electrode and joins the patient cable. The power cord and network cable connect the machine to the wall/network; the RL electrode is the ground.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: If the patient's prior ECG had electrodes in a slightly modified position, the best practice is to:
options: Always copy errors from the prior ECG
Use the standard positions and note any unavoidable modifications so the reader can compare
questions.explanation: Standard placement is the goal; documented modifications allow fair comparison. Copying errors or random placement defeats comparison, and skipping limb leads makes an incomplete ECG.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Most ECG machines acquire all 12 leads:
options: Only when the patient holds their breath
Simultaneously over the same 10 seconds, then print in a 3 × 4 format
One lead at a time over 2 minutes
questions.explanation: Modern digital machines record all leads at once; the printed columns show consecutive 2.5-second windows.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Where should V1 and V2 be placed if the patient has a pectus excavatum (sunken chest)?
options: At the 4th intercostal space beside the sternum as usual, noting any unusual anatomy
questions.explanation: Landmarks do not change; note anatomy that may affect the tracing. Moving to the 2nd ICS, the abdomen or the back would produce non-standard leads.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Lead aVR shows upright P, QRS and T waves on a patient with normal anatomy. You should first suspect:
questions.explanation: An upright aVR with inverted lead I is the classic sign of arm lead reversal. Pericarditis, hypokalemia and normal variants do not invert lead I and make aVR upright.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Which artifact is typically regular and occurs at a frequency of 60 Hz in North America?
questions.explanation: Electrical power in North America cycles at 60 Hz (50 Hz in many other countries). Tremor and muscle twitching are irregular; wandering baseline is a slow drift.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: The AC notch filter on an ECG machine is used to:
questions.explanation: A notch filter targets the power-line frequency; it does not fix poor electrode contact. Filters do not remove P waves, increase QRS amplitude or change paper speed.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: A patient with an insulin pump and a bedside fan has a fuzzy baseline in all leads. The most practical first step is:
options: Move or switch off nearby electrical devices (such as the fan) and route cables away from them
Ask the patient to hold their breath
questions.explanation: Remove sources of interference that are safe to turn off; never disconnect medical devices without an order.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Electrodes that have been left open on the cart for several days most commonly cause:
options: High impedance and noisy or wandering signals from dried gel
questions.explanation: Keep electrode packages sealed; dried gel increases impedance. Dried electrodes stick worse, not better, and cannot create hyperkalemia patterns or flutter.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Which leads make up the hexaxial reference system?
options: The six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF)
questions.explanation: The hexaxial system combines the three bipolar and three augmented limb leads in the frontal plane.
questions.source: Dubin, Rapid Interpretation of EKG's, 6th ed. (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Wilson's central terminal is used as the negative (reference) pole for:
questions.explanation: Precordial leads compare each chest electrode with a central terminal formed from the limb electrodes.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: When V1–V6 are mirrored on the right chest (V1R–V6R), V1R is placed at:
options: The 4th intercostal space, left sternal border (the usual V2 site)
questions.explanation: In mirror-image right-sided placement, V1R and V2R swap sides of the sternum; V3R–V6R mirror V3–V6 on the right.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Posterior lead V7 is placed at the:
options: Left posterior axillary line, level with V6
questions.explanation: V7 posterior axillary line, V8 mid-scapular line (tip of the scapula), V9 left paraspinal border.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Each vertical 5-mm large box at standard calibration equals:
questions.explanation: 10 mm = 1 mV, so 5 mm = 0.5 mV. 5 mV would be 50 mm, 0.05 mV is half a small box, and 1 mV is 10 mm.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Why must the calibration mark be checked before measuring voltage criteria such as LVH?
options: Voltage criteria assume 10 mm/mV; half or double standard changes measured heights
questions.explanation: At half standard, a QRS that looks 20 mm is really 40 mm (4 mV). The calibration mark does not set rate, lead placement or PR interval.
questions.source: Hancock et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part V: Chamber Hypertrophy (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Which findings suggest a technical problem rather than a true arrhythmia? (Select two.)
options: The disturbance appears in only some leads
Normal QRS complexes continue on time through the disturbance
The patient is unresponsive and pulseless
All leads show identical chaotic waves and the patient collapses
questions.explanation: Artifact usually affects selected leads and does not interrupt the underlying rhythm; clinical status confirms.
questions.source: Booth & O'Brien, Electrocardiography for Healthcare Professionals (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Put the chest electrode placement sequence in the recommended order.
items: V5 (anterior axillary line, level with V4)
questions.explanation: Place V4 before V3 because V3 is defined as the midpoint between V2 and V4. Placing V3 before V4 forces you to guess the midpoint.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: Which is the best practice for single-use (disposable) electrodes?
options: Use once and discard; never reuse on another patient
questions.explanation: Reusing electrodes risks infection and poor contact. Reusing, washing or storing opened packs dries the gel and spreads infection.
questions.source: CDC/HICPAC 2007 Guideline for Isolation Precautions

questions.stem: After acquiring the ECG, the most important quality check before removing electrodes is:
options: The paper is the right color
All 12 leads are present, labeled, free of significant artifact and the calibration is shown
questions.explanation: Checking the tracing before removing electrodes avoids repeat preps. Paper color, patient sleep or a specific heart rate do not determine tracing quality.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The bundle of His divides into the right bundle branch and the left bundle branch; the left bundle further divides into:
options: Right anterior and right posterior fascicles
Left anterior and left posterior fascicles
questions.explanation: The left bundle has anterior and posterior fascicles (and septal fibers); block of a fascicle shifts the axis.
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Left posterior fascicular block typically causes:
options: Right axis deviation (with other causes of RAD excluded)
questions.explanation: LPFB is uncommon and diagnosed when RAD (+90° to +180°) has no other explanation such as RVH.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: Which leads show reciprocal changes in an acute high-lateral (I, aVL) STEMI?
questions.explanation: Inferior and high lateral leads face opposite directions in the frontal plane, so each shows reciprocal change for the other.
questions.source: Wagner et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part VI: Acute Ischemia/Infarction (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: The Balke (Balke-Ware) treadmill protocol keeps speed constant and:
options: Uses 3-minute stages of the Bruce protocol
Increases the grade in small increments
questions.explanation: Balke protocols hold speed (e.g., 3.3 mph) and raise grade gradually—useful for deconditioned patients.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Ramp protocols differ from staged protocols because workload:
options: Is set only by the patient
Increases continuously in small steps rather than large jumps every few minutes
questions.explanation: Ramp protocols individualize the increase so maximal effort is reached in about 8–12 minutes.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Stage 0 of the Modified Bruce protocol is:
questions.explanation: Modified Bruce: 1.7 mph/0%, then 1.7 mph/5%, then joins standard Bruce stage 1 (1.7 mph/10%).
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The rate-pressure product (double product) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Double product is an index of myocardial oxygen demand. It uses systolic (not diastolic) pressure and is a product, not a ratio or a sum.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: At peak exercise, HR is 160 bpm and BP 180/80 mm Hg. The double product is:
questions.explanation: 160 × 180 = 28,800 (mm Hg × bpm). 160 × 80 = 12,800 uses the diastolic value by mistake; 340 is a sum.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A blunted heart-rate response (failure to reach 85% of predicted) without beta blockers is called:
questions.explanation: Chronotropic incompetence is associated with worse prognosis and should be noted. A hypertensive response refers to blood pressure; sinus arrhythmia is respiratory variation.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Heart-rate recovery is considered abnormal when heart rate falls by ≤ 12 bpm in the first minute of upright recovery (cool-down). Why is this monitored?
options: Slow heart-rate recovery is linked to higher mortality risk
questions.explanation: Heart-rate recovery reflects vagal reactivation and has prognostic value. Heart-rate recovery says nothing about lead placement, valve area or potassium.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: During a treadmill test, ECG monitoring should be:
options: Continuous, with recordings at the end of each stage, at peak, and during recovery
Only if the patient has symptoms
questions.explanation: Continuous monitoring allows prompt recognition of ischemia or arrhythmias. Intermittent monitoring would miss ischemia or arrhythmias between checks.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which emergency drug should be available for symptomatic bradycardia in a stress lab?
questions.explanation: Emergency carts in stress labs stock ACLS drugs including atropine, epinephrine and amiodarone.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Treadmill calibration of speed and grade should be checked:
options: Regularly per the manufacturer and lab quality program
questions.explanation: Inaccurate speed or grade makes METs and protocol staging incorrect. Waiting for complaints or a fall means tests may already have been staged incorrectly.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Most patients report symptoms using which scale for chest pain during stress testing?
options: Angina scale (e.g., 1 = mild to 4 = most severe)
questions.explanation: An angina scale standardizes reporting of chest pain severity. Glasgow, Apgar and Braden scales measure consciousness, newborn status and pressure-injury risk.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which are RELATIVE indications to stop exercise? (Select two.)
options: Increasing chest pain that is not yet severe
Signs of poor perfusion such as cyanosis
questions.explanation: Increasing chest pain and fatigue/claudication are relative; sustained VT, patient request and poor perfusion are absolute.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: During recovery, the patient's ECG develops 2.5 mm downsloping ST depression that was not present at peak. This is:
options: Significant—ischemic changes can appear in recovery; continue monitoring and inform the physician
questions.explanation: Recovery-phase ST depression is diagnostically important. Ending exercise does not make ischemic changes irrelevant, and restarting exercise is unsafe.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Exercise-induced hypotension (SBP drops below resting during exercise) is concerning because it may indicate:
options: Severe coronary disease or left ventricular dysfunction
questions.explanation: A fall in SBP with increasing workload suggests inability to increase cardiac output and is an indication to stop.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is a RELATIVE contraindication to exercise testing?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with resting outflow obstruction
questions.explanation: HCM with outflow tract obstruction is relative; the others are absolute contraindications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which is a RELATIVE contraindication to exercise testing?
questions.explanation: High-degree AV block, tachy- or bradyarrhythmias and electrolyte abnormalities are relative contraindications.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Why are electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., potassium 2.8 mEq/L) a concern before exercise testing?
options: They increase arrhythmia risk and can cause ST-T changes that confuse interpretation
questions.explanation: Electrolyte abnormalities are a relative contraindication. Electrolyte problems do not improve capacity or affect the treadmill.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which stress test is often preferred in patients with LBBB or ventricular pacing?
questions.explanation: Exercise and dobutamine can cause false septal perfusion defects in LBBB; vasodilator stress reduces this.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: During dobutamine stress, the dose is typically increased every:
options: 3 minutes in stages until target heart rate or an endpoint
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is titrated in 3-minute stages (e.g., 5–10 up to 40–50 mcg/kg/min), with atropine added if needed.
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: In a "low-level" exercise test after an MI, the test is usually stopped at:
options: A predetermined endpoint such as about 5–6 METs or a heart rate of about 120 bpm (or 70% of predicted)
questions.explanation: Submaximal post-MI tests use conservative endpoints for risk stratification. Maximal or 100% predicted endpoints are not used soon after MI, and time alone is not the endpoint.
questions.source: Gibbons et al., ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing

questions.stem: Before nuclear imaging, why might a patient be asked to fast?
options: To reduce gut (subdiaphragmatic) tracer activity and nausea during stress
questions.explanation: Fasting for a few hours is common practice; follow the lab's protocol (diabetics receive specific instructions).
questions.source: Henzlova et al., ASNC Imaging Guidelines for SPECT Nuclear Cardiology: Stress Protocols (J Nucl Cardiol 2016)

questions.stem: A patient finishes the test and wants to drive home immediately while still sweaty and lightheaded. You should:
options: Give them coffee and send them out
Keep them in the lab for observation until symptoms resolve and the physician clears them
Tell them to jog to cool down
questions.explanation: Patients are discharged only after recovery and physician clearance. Sending a symptomatic patient away or having them jog is unsafe.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Which shoes are best for a treadmill test?
options: Comfortable, closed-toe walking or running shoes
questions.explanation: Proper footwear prevents slipping and injury. High heels, flip-flops and bare feet risk slipping and injury.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: A patient on the treadmill starts to stumble and grab the rails. The technician should:
options: Be ready to support the patient and stop the treadmill if the patient cannot continue safely
questions.explanation: Safety comes first; staff stand close to the patient and the stop button. Speeding up, increasing grade or stepping away could cause a fall.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: Put the steps in order when an absolute endpoint occurs during exercise.
items: Stop the treadmill (or slow to a stop per protocol)
Assist the patient to a supine or seated position
Continue ECG and blood pressure monitoring
Notify the physician and document the event
questions.explanation: Stop exercise, position safely, keep monitoring and get the physician; document the endpoint and findings.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: The standard treadmill metric "% grade" refers to:
questions.explanation: Grade expresses incline; Bruce protocol raises grade 2% per stage from 10% to 22%. Belt speed is measured in mph; effort uses the Borg scale; heart-rate reserve is a separate calculation.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: An external loop recorder continuously records and saves:
options: Only the next 30 seconds after activation
Nothing until the device is returned
A window of ECG before and after the patient activates it (or an auto-trigger)
questions.explanation: Loop memory keeps pre-event ECG, capturing the onset of brief arrhythmias. Loop recorders keep pre-activation data, unlike devices that start recording only after the button is pressed.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Which item is given to the patient at Holter hook-up?
questions.explanation: Diaries record time-stamped symptoms and activities. Treadmill schedules, defibrillators and prescriptions are not part of Holter hook-up.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: If a patient has a large amount of chest hair, before applying Holter electrodes you should:
options: Clip the hair at the sites (clippers rather than razors when possible)
questions.explanation: Hair prevents adhesion; clipping reduces nicks compared with shaving. Electrodes do not stick over hair; lotion worsens adhesion; tape alone does not fix poor contact.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: A Holter tracing shows periods of very low amplitude in all channels during the night. A likely cause is:
options: Patient position changes affecting electrode contact or recorder function—check the diary and electrode adhesion
questions.explanation: Body position can shift the signal; persistent loss suggests technical issues. VF all night would not be compatible with a normal morning; calibration at 20 mm/mV would make complexes larger.
questions.source: Steinberg et al., ISHNE-HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Ambulatory ECG and External Cardiac Monitoring (2017)

questions.stem: Which drug class is most associated with QT prolongation as a common side effect, requiring ECG monitoring when started in the hospital?
options: Class III antiarrhythmics such as sotalol and dofetilide
questions.explanation: Sotalol and dofetilide are typically started with in-hospital ECG/QT monitoring because of torsades risk.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Amlodipine and nifedipine (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) mainly:
options: Dilate arteries to lower blood pressure, with little direct effect on AV conduction
questions.explanation: Dihydropyridines (-dipine) are vascular-selective; diltiazem and verapamil act more on the heart.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Which drug is given intravenously to convert or rate-control atrial fibrillation and also slows the AV node?
questions.explanation: IV diltiazem (a non-dihydropyridine CCB) is commonly used for AF rate control. Atropine and epinephrine speed the heart; aminophylline reverses vasodilator stress agents.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: A patient taking digoxin and furosemide has low potassium. Why is this concerning?
options: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and arrhythmias
questions.explanation: Potassium loss from diuretics increases digoxin binding and toxicity risk. Low potassium does not protect against toxicity and does not shorten the PR interval.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Amiodarone is used for:
options: Ventricular and atrial arrhythmias, including VF/pulseless VT in ACLS
questions.explanation: Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO is given for shock-refractory VF/pVT; it is also used for AF. It is not a treatment for bradycardia, hypotension or hyperkalemia.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Clopidogrel and aspirin are:
questions.explanation: Antiplatelets prevent platelet aggregation (e.g., after stents). They do not change ECG intervals.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Statins (e.g., atorvastatin) are used to:
options: Lower cholesterol (LDL) and reduce cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: Statins are lipid-lowering agents without direct ECG effects. Statins do not slow the heart rate, treat VT or shorten the QT interval.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic. Which ECG change could develop if potassium rises too high?
questions.explanation: Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors and ARBs can cause hyperkalemia. U waves suggest LOW potassium; short PR and delta waves suggest pre-excitation.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Dopamine or epinephrine infusions may be used in bradycardia when:
options: Atropine is ineffective and the patient remains symptomatic (as an alternative or bridge to pacing)
questions.explanation: AHA bradycardia algorithm: atropine first, then transcutaneous pacing or dopamine/epinephrine infusion.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Which antiarrhythmic class consists of beta blockers?
questions.explanation: Vaughan Williams: I sodium channel blockers; II beta blockers; III potassium channel blockers; IV calcium channel blockers.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Sinus tachycardia in a patient using albuterol inhalers is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: Beta-agonists can raise heart rate. Beta blockade slows the heart; digoxin toxicity and hypercalcemia do not typically cause sinus tachycardia.
questions.source: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed) for the named drug

questions.stem: Which statement about adenosine given for SVT is correct?
options: It is given slowly over 30 minutes
It is given as a rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush because its half-life is very short
questions.explanation: Rapid push (6 mg, then 12 mg if needed) with flush ensures the drug reaches the heart. A slow infusion would let the drug be metabolized before reaching the heart; it is IV only and is not an asystole treatment.
questions.source: AHA 2020 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: Sinus rhythm, normal axis (lead I and aVF positive), narrow QRS, normal R-wave progression and no ST elevation or depression. Why not left ventricular hypertrophy with strain? That pattern would show: very tall voltages (S V1 + R V5/V6 ≥ 35 mm) with lateral ST depression/T inversion (strain).
questions.source: Wagner & Strauss, Marriott's Practical Electrocardiography (CCI reference)

questions.stem: Using leads I and aVF (and II if needed), what is the QRS axis?

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: QRS ≥ 0.12 s with a terminal R' in V1 and wide terminal S waves in I and V6; the T waves in V1–V2 are often inverted (secondary change). Why not left bundle branch block? That pattern would show: qRS ≥ 0.12 s, deep QS/rS in V1–V2, broad R waves without septal q in I, aVL, V5–V6, with discordant ST-T changes.
questions.source: Surawicz et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: This 12-lead was just recorded on a patient whose prior ECG was normal. What best explains the appearance?
questions.explanation: Lead I is inverted (negative P, QRS and T) and aVR is upright—classic LA/RA reversal. Leads II and III and aVR/aVL are swapped. Correct the electrode placement and repeat the ECG. Why not dextrocardia? That pattern would show: lead I shows inverted P, QRS and T with aVR upright, and R waves get smaller from V1 to V6 instead of larger.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: You suspect electrode misplacement on this tracing. What should you do?
options: Report it as an acute MI
Delete the leads that look abnormal
Check and correct electrode placement, then repeat the ECG and label it as a repeat
Send it as is—the computer will correct it
questions.explanation: Lead I is inverted (negative P, QRS and T) and aVR is upright—classic LA/RA reversal. Leads II and III and aVR/aVL are swapped. Reversals can mimic infarction or axis deviation, so the tracing must be repeated with correct placement.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: No P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm in the lead II rhythm strip, with a fibrillatory baseline and narrow QRS complexes. Why not normal 12-lead ecg? That pattern would show: sinus rhythm, normal axis (lead I and aVF positive), narrow QRS, normal R-wave progression and no ST elevation or depression.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this 12-lead ECG?
questions.explanation: Pacing spikes precede wide QRS complexes in every beat; the paced QRS looks LBBB-like with a superior axis because pacing starts at the right ventricular apex. Why not left bundle branch block? That pattern would show: qRS ≥ 0.12 s, deep QS/rS in V1–V2, broad R waves without septal q in I, aVL, V5–V6, with discordant ST-T changes.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this 12-lead ECG?

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Atrial flutter: regular sawtooth F waves at about 250–350 per minute (classically ~300), best seen in II, III, aVF; the ventricles respond in a ratio such as 2:1, 3:1 or 4:1. Source description: "The arrows mark the atrial flutter waves. This is an example of an alternating 2:1 and 3:1 block." (CardioNetworks ECGpedia contributors, CC BY-SA 3.0).

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic, irregular deflections with no identifiable P, QRS or T waves—no cardiac output. Source description: "CardioNetworks ECGpedia." (CardioNetworks ECGpedia contributor (Googletrans), CC BY-SA 3.0).
questions.source: File:De-Rhythm ventricular fibrillation (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).png — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De-Rhythm_ventricular_fibrillation_(CardioNetworks_ECGpedia).png

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: RBBB: QRS ≥ 0.12 s with an rSR' pattern in V1 (terminal R'), and wide S waves in I and V6. Source description: "ECG of a 78-year-old female with normal sinus rhythm and right bundle branch block. The heart rate is 74 bpm. QRS width 130 ms. QT/QTc 432/479 ms." (Ewingdo, CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Sinus arrest/pause: the SA node fails to fire, so a complete P–QRS–T is missing and the pause is not an exact multiple of the P–P interval. Source description: "Telemetry monitor rhythm strip of a 44-year-old female. Rhythm strip demonstrates sinus node dysfunction or sinus pause with the first sinus pause lasting 2.8 s" (PerpetuallyTachy, CC BY-SA 4.0).
questions.source: File:ECG Sinus Pause.jpg — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ECG_Sinus_Pause.jpg

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
options: Sinus rhythm with type II (Mobitz II) second-degree AV block
questions.explanation: Second-degree AV block Mobitz II: the PR is constant on conducted beats, and P waves are suddenly not conducted; the QRS is often wide. Source description: "Sinus rhythm (rate = 100/min) with 3:2 and 2:1 Type II A-V block; RBBB." (Jer5150, CC BY-SA 3.0).
questions.source: File:Sinus rhythm with 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 Type II A-V block.png — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sinus_rhythm_with_3-to-2_and_2-to-1_Type_II_A-V_block.png

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm: regular, rate 60–100, an upright P before every QRS, PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS < 0.12 s. Source description: "I captured this 12 lead ECG from a friend of mine during a training class at the fire station." (MoodyGroove, Public domain).
questions.source: File:12 lead ECG of a 26 year old male.jpg — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:12_lead_ECG_of_a_26_year_old_male.jpg

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Third-degree (complete) AV block: P waves and QRS complexes are independent (AV dissociation); atrial rate is faster than the ventricular escape rate; PR intervals vary randomly. Source description: "Two EKG strips obtained in the same patient simultaneously (each represents a different vector of the heart’s electrical conduction), demonstrating complete AV " (Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, FACC, CC BY 3.0).
questions.source: File:3rd degree heart block.PNG — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:3rd_degree_heart_block.PNG

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
options: Sinus rhythm with a unifocal PVC
Sinus rhythm with a PVC couplet
questions.explanation: Ventricular bigeminy: every other beat is a PVC (normal, PVC, normal, PVC…). Source description: "A rhythm strip demonstrating bigeminy" (James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0).
questions.source: File:Bigeminy2010.JPG — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bigeminy2010.JPG

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Dual-chamber (AV) pacing: an atrial spike before the P wave and a ventricular spike before each wide QRS. Source description: "Dual chamber pacemaker ECG. 77-years-old man with congestive heart failure." (Jmarchn, CC0).
questions.source: File:DualChamberPacemaker ECG 3x4.jpg — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DualChamberPacemaker_ECG_3x4.jpg

questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: LBBB: QRS ≥ 0.12 s with a deep QS or rS in V1 and broad R waves in I, aVL, V5–V6 without septal q waves. Source description: "Elektrokardiogram pri poruche prevodu srdcových vzruchov (blokáda ľavého Tawarovho ramienka). questions.stem: This is a real ECG recording (licensed from Wikimedia Commons). What does it show?
questions.explanation: Junctional escape rhythm: regular, narrow QRS, rate 40–60; P waves are inverted before the QRS (PR < 0.12 s), hidden, or after the QRS. Source description: "This is an example of an ECG with junctional rhythm. This is characterized by regular rhythm with absent or inverted or mistimed P waves." (Dhaval Desai, MD, MPH, CC BY-SA 4.0).
questions.source: File:ECG of Junctional Rhythm.png — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ECG_of_Junctional_Rhythm.png

options: Sinus rhythm with a unifocal PVC
questions.explanation: A PVC is an early, wide (≥ 0.12 s), bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave, a T wave opposite the QRS and usually a full compensatory pause. Source description: "A premature ventricular contraction marked by the arrow." (James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old is scheduled for a treadmill test. Using 220 − age, what is 85% of the age-predicted maximum heart rate?
questions.explanation: APMHR = 220 − 25 = 195 bpm; 85% × 195 = 165.8 ≈ 166 bpm. 195 is the full predicted maximum, not the 85% target.
questions.source: Fletcher et al., Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, AHA Scientific Statement (Circulation 2013)

questions.stem: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, an interval spans 5 small boxes. How long is it?
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s each 1-mm box = 0.04 s, so 5 × 0.04 = 0.20 s. A common error is using 0.02 s (the 50 mm/s value) per box or counting large boxes (0.20 s each).
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The calibration is set at 10 mm/mV. An R wave is 15 mm tall. What is its true amplitude?
questions.explanation: Amplitude = height ÷ calibration = 15 mm ÷ 10 mm/mV = 1.5 mV. At standard calibration every 10 mm (two large boxes) equals 1 mV.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The calibration is set at 5 mm/mV. An R wave is 8 mm tall. What is its true amplitude?
questions.explanation: Amplitude = height ÷ calibration = 8 mm ÷ 5 mm/mV = 1.6 mV. Assuming the standard 10 mm/mV here would give the wrong value, so always check the calibration mark.
questions.source: Kligfield et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for Standardization of the ECG, Part I (Circulation 2007)

questions.stem: The QT interval is 0.36 s and the R–R interval is 0.64 s. Using Bazett's formula, what is the QTc?
questions.explanation: QTc = QT ÷ √RR = 0.36 ÷ √0.64 = 0.36 ÷ 0.80 ≈ 0.45 s. This is within normal limits.
questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)

questions.stem: The QT interval is 0.40 s and the R–R interval is 1.00 s. Using Bazett's formula, what is the QTc?
questions.explanation: QTc = QT ÷ √RR = 0.40 ÷ √1.00 = 0.40 ÷ 1.00 ≈ 0.40 s. This is within normal limits.
questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)

questions.source: Rautaharju et al., AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part IV: ST Segment, T and U Waves, and the QT Interval (Circulation 2009)
